3.7 Multi-agent reinforcement learning framework
While the preceding sections have detailed the environment’s design, this subsection describes the MARL framework responsible for training the agents’ policies. A significant contribution of our work is the framework’s native support for comparing different MARL training and inference paradigms, which is essential for studying the trade-offs between centralization and decentralization in learning and control. This is a core research instrument that allows for the rigorous, side-by-side evaluation of coordination strategies under varying degrees of information sharing and architectural constraints. The entire training and inference pipeline is managed by a dedicated Trainer Module and Inference Module, respectively, built upon established libraries like Ray RLlib [51], to ensure robustness, scalability, and reproducibility.
A detailed treatment of the MARL framework, including its full mathematical and implementation specifics, is reserved for a forthcoming paper; the following serves as a comprehensive overview of its key components and capabilities.
3.7.1 Training and execution paradigms
A primary research objective of this work is to evaluate the performance and scalability of different levels of decentralization. To this end, the framework is designed to seamlessly implement and compare three canonical MARL paradigms, each offering a unique balance of performance, scalability, and real-world deployability.
• Centralized Training, Centralized Execution (CTCE): In this paradigm, a single, centralized policy has access to the full global state (concatenated observations of all agents) and outputs a joint action for all agents simultaneously. This model serves as a theoretical upper bound for system performance, as it represents the ideal of perfect information and fully coordinated execution. While often intractable in real-world systems due to its violation of decentralization principles and exponential scaling challenges, it provides a benchmark for quantifying the performance gap between the theoretical optimum and more practical, decentralized approaches.
• Centralized Training, Decentralized Execution (CTDE): This is a popular and practical paradigm that represents a hybrid approach. Agent policies are trained offline in a centralized simulator with access to global information (e.g., the states and actions of other agents, centralized critics). This allows the learning algorithm to solve the credit assignment problem and learn complex, coordinated strategies. During inference, however, each agent’s policy operates in a fully decentralized manner, relying only on its own local observation. This approach is highly compelling because it allows for sophisticated, coordinated strategies to be learned offline while still producing policies that are deployable in a realistic, decentralized setting without requiring a central controller at runtime.
Decentralized Training, Decentralized Execution (DTDE): This represents the fully decentralized ideal, most closely mirroring the constraints of many real-world systems. Each agent learns its policy independently, based only on its own stream of local observations and rewards, without a centralized training coordinator. This paradigm is highly scalable and robust to single points of failure. However, it faces significant theoretical challenges related to the non-stationarity of the environment (as other agents’ policies are constantly changing) and the difficulty of credit assignment. Our framework’s focus on implicit cooperation through shared KPI signals in the observation and reward functions is specifically designed to address these challenges and make DTDE a more viable and effective approach.
3.7.2 Reinforcement learning algorithms and infrastructure
The framework integrates with high-performance RL libraries to implement the learning algorithms. While the modular design is algorithm-agnostic, our experiments primarily leverage state-of-the-art policy gradient and actor-critic methods suitable for multi-agent environments and continuous action spaces. We highlight three implemented algorithms:
• Proximal policy optimization (PPO): A robust on-policy algorithm recognized for its stability and sample efficiency [52]. Its core innovation is a clipped objective function that prevents destructively large policy updates, making it a strong and reliable baseline for complex control tasks.
Asynchronous proximal policy optimization (APPO): APPO enhances scalability for distributed training through off-policy corrections (V-trace), which allows the algorithm to learn from off-policy data more effectively [52]. This is particularly valuable in multi-agent environments where agents may have different learning rates and exploration strategies, leading to off-policy data that standard PPO cannot handle efficiently.
• Soft actor-critic (SAC): An off-policy algorithm that encourages exploration by adding an entropy bonus to the objective [53]. This principled approach to balancing exploration and exploitation makes it highly effective in continuous control tasks, often leading to more robust and performant final policies, which is particularly valuable for discovering novel coordination strategies in the LEM.
To manage the complexity of large-scale MARL experiments, the training infrastructure incorporates advanced techniques such as Population-Based Training [54], which is a hybrid approach that jointly optimizes the neural network weights and hyperparameters of a population of agents, dynamically allocating computational resources to the most promising training runs. This automates the difficult process of hyperparameter tuning and often leads to more robust and higher-performing final policies, which is particularly beneficial in the non-stationary context of MARL. The entire experimental workflow, from training and checkpointing to metrics collection and final inference, is managed to ensure reproducibility and rigorous scientific comparison.
3.8 Analytics and visualizations
An Analytics Module and a Visualization Module are integrated into the framework, providing a suite of tools for processing, analyzing, and plotting the high-dimensional data generated during simulation runs. This module is essential for moving beyond raw numerical outputs to a qualitative understanding of the emergent dynamics within the LEM.
The visualization capabilities are categorized to provide distinct perspectives on the simulation outcomes:
• Analysis of social and relational dynamics: To investigate the emergence of trading relationships and market structure, the framework can generate a trading network figure. In this plot, agents are rendered as nodes in a graph, and the executed trades are represented as edges connecting them. The thickness of an edge is proportional to the total volume of energy traded between the two agents, and the grayscale tone of each edge represents the distance between the agents, providing a visualization of the market’s social fabric. This allows for the direct observation of how stable trading coalitions and preferred partnerships evolve over time.
Economic performance analysis: To understand the statistical properties of market outcomes, the Visualization Module can generate price and volume distribution plots. These histograms and kernel density estimates reveal the distribution of market clearing prices and trade volumes, offering insights into price stability, market liquidity, and the overall efficiency of price discovery under different market mechanisms.
• Spatio-temporal pattern recognition: To analyze the physical dimension of market activity, a spatial distribution of trading activity plot can be generated. This visualization renders the grid topology as a heatmap, where the color intensity of different nodes or areas corresponds to the volume of trading activity. This is particularly useful for identifying the emergence of localized trading hubs and for correlating economic activity with physical grid phenomena, such as congestion.
• Performance dashboards: For a high-level, comparative overview of different experimental scenarios, the framework provides a suite of metrics dashboards. These composite plots summarize the most critical KPIs from the Analytics Module into a single, easily digestible format. Dedicated dashboards are available for grid stability, economic efficiency, resource utilization, and DSO performance, allowing researchers to quickly assess and compare the multi-faceted outcomes of their experiments.
3.9 Complete simulation workflow
The preceding sections have detailed the individual components of the framework; this final subsection elucidates how these modules are orchestrated into a complete, end-to-end simulation loop. The step method within the LEM environment manages this sequence of operations, ensuring that data flows logically between the agents, market, grid, and coordination modules at each discrete trading period
t \in \{ 1 , \ldots , \tau \}
. Understanding this workflow is essential for appreciating how the framework maintains state consistency and facilitates the agent learning process. The entire process at each trading period
t \in \{ 1 , \ldots , \tau \}
is conceptualized as a sequence of eight distinct phases, from initial agent decision to the final observation and reward feedback
( \mathrm { s e e }   \mathrm { F i g } ,   3 )
A detailed breakdown of the simulation process is as follows:
Action processing and validation: The workflow begins with the raw action received from the MARL policies. For each agent, the first and most critical step is to ground its intended action in physical reality. Agents limit each action based on the current generation, demand, and the agent’s battery state. Subsequently, the Action Module performs a rule-based validation, ensuring the action’s components (price, quantity, buy/sell, partner) fall within the predefined market bounds. This two-step validation ensures that only physically and economically plausible actions proceed to the next phase.
Order creation and market submission: Validated actions are then formatted into formal orders. If the agent’s policy is not directly controlling partner choice, a rule-based selection method can be invoked here, scoring potential partners based on reputation and grid distance. This phase culminates in a collection of structured orders ready for market submission.
Market clearing and trade execution: The collection of orders is passed to the Market Module which executes its three-stage clearing process: it first attempts to match mutually preferred partners, then processes the remaining orders through the price-based double auction (factoring in reputation scores), and finally clears any residual unmatched orders with the DSO. The output of this phase is a list of all executed trades and summary statistics.
Energy tracking and battery updates: The list of all executed trades is used to update the physical state of each agent (e.g., internal energy tracking variables and change in the battery’s SoC), and grid state (e.g., balance and congestion).
Reward calculation and KPI updates: With the economic and physical outcomes of the trading period
t \in \{ 1 , \ldots , \tau \}
now determined, the Implicit Cooperation Module gathers all necessary data (trades, agent states, grid conditions) to compute the full suite of system-level KPIs. These KPIs are then passed to the reward function, which calculates the final, composite reward for each agent, combining their individual performance with the cooperation bonuses derived from the system-wide KPIs.
State transitions and environment updates: This phase advances the simulation’s global state, and the environment’s internal clock is incremented. Crucially, agent-level states that depend on the full market outcome, such as financial balances and reputation scores, are updated based on the results from the Reputation Module.
Observation update and information sharing: The Observation Module constructs the next local observation for each agent
( o _ { i , t + 1 } \in O _ { i } )
. This new observation vector is assembled from the newly updated environment state, including the agent’s private information, public market signals, and the system-level KPIs calculated in Phase 5. This step closes the information loop, providing agents with the feedback necessary for their next decision.
Episode management and termination: Finally, the environment checks for termination conditions (e.g., reaching the maximum number of trading periods 𝜏 for the episode). If the episode has not concluded, the environment returns the newly generated observations and computed rewards to the MARL algorithm, and the entire workflow repeats for trading period
t + 1 \in \{ 1 , \ldots , \tau \}
This orchestrated workflow ensures that every agent’s action influences the market and grid, the collective outcome is measured and translated into shared signals (KPIs), and those signals are then used to inform and incentivize the agents’ decisions in the subsequent trading period. This constitutes the core feedback loop that enables the study of emergent, implicit cooperation within a complex, decentralized system.

4.1 Case study: battery storage coordination
This case study showcase and analyzes the role of battery energy storage systems in decentralized LEMs, leveraging the framework’s integrated models.
The primary goal is to analyze how different battery configurations and deployment strategies affect the emergence of implicit coordination among agents (MARL or otherwise), influence overall market efficiency (e.g., price volatility, social welfare), and contribute to grid stability through enhanced flexibility.
The simulation environment is configured with 7 agents operating on a 24-hour daily cycle in a grid network with a mesh topology and a nominal capacity of 1200 kW. A bid-ask spread clearing mechanism is employed, chosen specifically because the inherent difference between buy and sell prices creates clear economic incentives for storage arbitrage, thus highlighting the value that agents learn (or exploit, if they do not learn) from their batteries. The market allows for a wide price range (i.e., 35-280 $/MWh) and quantity range (i.e., 0.1-200 kWh) to accommodate storage-driven strategies.
In this paper we showcase two distinct scenarios (although readers can find six comprehensive scenarios in the dedicated GitHub repository), each featuring agents with the same base generation capacity (i.e., 60 kW, with some random variation) and associated profiles but with differences in the deployment of their batteries:
No battery:
A baseline scenario establishing performance without any storage flexibility, forcing agents into real-time market participation only. All agents are configured to have no battery.
Strategic battery:
Explores deployment where agent profiles (generation/demand timing) and storage capabilities (varying ratios 0.5-1.2, high 95% efficiency) are specifically designed a priori to facilitate coordinated load balancing and time-shifting across the community (e.g., agents with morning generation peaks paired with storage potentially serving agents with evening demand peaks).
4.2 Baseline models
To evaluate the performance achieved by the agents within case study, the following baselines are essential for establishing context:
•
Zero-intelligence agents:
This baseline serves as a lower bound on performance. Agents operate without any learning or strategic foresight. At each time step, they submit random bids using a uniform random distribution within price bounds that are valid within the market’s price and quantity limits and respect their individual physical constraints (e.g., battery SoC, generation availability). Comparing MARL performance (when trained) against this baseline demonstrates that learned policies are non-trivial and achieve meaningful economic and coordination outcomes beyond random chance. For the purposes of clarity and demonstration of the capabilities of the framework, the results presented in Section 5 will utilize these zero-intelligence agents to illustrate the impact of different configurations (e.g., battery scenarios).
MARL with CTCE paradigm:
As detailed in Section 3.7.1, this paradigm acts as a theoretical upper bound within the context of the MARL algorithms used. A single policy, trained with access to the full global state and controlling all agents simultaneously using the same underlying MARL algorithm (e.g., PPO, APPO or SAC), represents the best achievable performance under conditions of perfect information and perfect coordination attainable by that algorithm. Comparing decentralized execution results (CTDE or DTDE) against the CTCE benchmark allows for quantifying the performance degradation attributable to partial observability and independent decision making inherent in decentralized execution. While full MARL training is deferred to future work (see Section 6), this benchmark remains relevant for contextualizing potential performance.

5 Results and discussion
This section presents the analytical capabilities and techno-economic sensitivity of the proposed simulation framework. As outlined in Section 4, the findings presented here are generated using the zero-intelligence agent baseline. By comparing the no battery and strategic battery scenarios using non-learning agents that operate under randomized but valid heuristics, we can demonstrate the framework’s high-fidelity modeling. This allows us to observe how the physics of the system (the market rules, grid constraints, and agent asset configurations) shape the outcomes, independent of the learned MARL policies. The results from full MARL training, which constitutes the next work of this research, are detailed in Section 6.
5.1 Framework capability demonstration
The core capability of the framework is its ability to quantify the systemic impact of different physical asset configurations. By simulating and contrasting these two scenarios, we can observe how the presence and strategic deployment of storage fundamentally alter market outcomes, even when agent behavior is non-strategic.
5.1.1 Price volatility and market stability
A primary function of a battery is temporal arbitrage (buying low and selling high) which stabilizes prices. Our framework captures this economic-physical interaction. Fig. 4 presents a comparative of the statistical distribution of P2P market clearing prices over the 24-hour simulation for both scenarios of the case study.
The no battery scenario (see Fig. 4a) serves as a baseline and shows a volatile market. The price distribution is multi-modal, with at two distinct price clusters. This is statistical evidence of a fractured market, where agents are entirely subject to the temporal mismatch between generation driving low prices (e.g., the cluster near 140 $/MWh) and demand driving high prices (e.g., the cluster near 230 $/MWh). The mean of $173.6 is pulled away from the median of $157.5, further indicating a skewed and unstable market.
The strategic battery scenario (see Fig. 4b) demonstrates a transformation of the market structure. The distribution becomes unimodal in a stable price regime that approximates a normal distribution. This is quantitatively confirmed by the fact that the mean of $152.2 and median of $158.5 are now almost identical, which is a feature of a symmetrical, stable, and predictable market.
This result demonstrates that the mere presence of strategically configured battery acts as a stabilizing asset, even with non-intelligent agents. The battery provides temporal flexibility, allowing the market to bridge the gap between high-generation and high-demand periods. This arbitrage effectively clips the price extremes and allows the market to converge to a stable clearing price. This finding validates the framework’s high-fidelity techno-economic model, proving its capability to capture the emergent, systemic effects that physical assets have on market dynamics.
5.1.2 Grid stability and system coordination
The framework’s Implicit Cooperation Module is designed to quantify system stability by measuring the supply-demand imbalance and calculating the coordination score as defined in (23). To illustrate this, Fig. 5 and Fig. 6 shows the net grid imbalance and the P2P trading ratio over the 24-hour simulation cycle, respectively.
The no battery scenario shows a volatile imbalance profile, mirroring the temporal mismatch between generation and demand. This forces a heavy and continuous reliance on the DSO to act as a sink or source, resulting in a low coordination core.
The strategic battery scenario demonstrates a smoother net load profile with a higher overall coordination score. The agents’ batteries, even when operated by zero-intelligence policies, provide a passive damper that absorbs systemic disturbances. The design of the strategic battery scenario (i.e., agents with morning generation and storage, agents with evening demand and storage) creates a natural, system-wide complementarity.
5.1.3 Market structure and economic efficiency
Beyond scalar metrics, the framework’s Visualization Module provides insights into the structure of the market. Fig. 7 illus trates the structural changes to the market’s social and spatial characteristics enabled by storage.
Fig. 7 visualizes the P2P trading network, where nodes represent agents and edges represent the volume of trade between them. The no battery scenario (see Fig. 7a) depicts a market where most agents (blue nodes) are in a net-demand state, forced to buy all their energy from the DSO (main seller). This demonstrates a market with no liquidity, no self-sufficiency, and a low volume of P2P trading.
The strategic battery scenario (see Fig. 7b) shows that agents have mostly differentiated into clear roles (i.e., agents with morning/afternoon generation are net sellers, agents with evening demand are net buyers), and trade more with each other. This indicates that the temporal flexibility from batteries has created the market. Furthermore, the role of the DSO has reversed from being the main seller in the no battery scenario to being the main buyer. This result showcases the LEM has transitioned from a state of energy deficit, dependent on the external grid, to a state of self-sufficiency and is now a net exporter of its surplus. This validation proves the framework’s ability to capture systemic changes in market structure and economic flow.
5.2 Discussion
The results from the zero-intelligence agent simulations validate the framework’s design, demonstrating that the underlying techno-economic model is sufficiently high-fidelity to capture the impact of physical asset configurations on market and grid performance. Table 2 presents a quantitative summary comparing the no battery and strategic battery scenarios, focusing on the aggregate agent rewards, which serve as a proxy for overall market viability and agent profitability.
The strategic battery scenario achieves a positive average aggregate reward of +42929.5, a reversal from the baseline’s large negative reward of -61556.1. This demonstrates the economic and systemic value that strategically deployed storage resources, even when operated non-strategically, provide to the market ecosystem by enabling temporal arbitrage. This validation provides a testbed for quantifying the value of different system designs and physical assets.

The framework is proven to be sensitive to the physical prerequisites for coordination (i.e., storage); the strategic battery scenario, for instance, creates clear, complementary roles that are ideal for future MARL agents to learn to fill. While this study held the market mechanism constant, the influence of storage on price volatility directly demonstrates the framework’s capability to analyze the coupling between market mechanisms and physical assets. Furthermore, this case study directly addresses the impact of physical grid constraints. The battery parameters (e.g., SoC or efficiency) are a form of temporal physical constraint, and their presence influences agent behavior and market outcomes, validating the framework’s capacity to test the market-versus-grid dichotomy.
While the presented 7-agent study validates the framework’s functional capabilities, a formal quantitative scalability analysis remains a critical component of future work. This would involve executing simulations with increasing agent populations (e.g., 10, 50, 100+ agents) to plot computational time and analyze the impact of agent count on market KPIs, thereby testing the framework’s performance under load.
We must reiterate that the results presented in this paper are illustrative and employ a zero-intelligence agent baseline to validate the simulation framework’s capability. A full MARL training is required to understand the emergent behavioral dynamics and the full potential of implicit cooperation (authors will publish this work in a forthcoming paper).

Finally, as with all simulations, the component models are abstractions that require continuous validation and calibration against real-world data to improve their fidelity.
6 Conclusion and future work
In this paper, we have presented a novel, open-source simulation framework specifically designed for the study of decentralized LEMs using MARL. Addressing a gap in the current landscape of energy simulation tools, specifically the lack of a unified platform that integrates realistic market mechanisms, physical grid constraints, and advanced MARL capabilities within a standardized and decentralized paradigm, our framework provides a robust, extensible, and Gymnasium-compliant environment for researching the complex dynamics of future energy systems.
The primary contribution is the LEM simulation framework itself. Its architecture and formulation as a Dec-POMDP overcomes the prevalent market-versus-grid dichotomy by cohesively unifying a modular market platform (featuring a hybrid preference/price-based matching and reputation systems) with a physically grounded grid model (incorporating transmission losses and congestion management). The framework is architected to support and facilitate research into fully decentralized learning and execution paradigms, moving beyond the limitations of centralized training assumptions common in prior work.

A second key contribution is the framework’s explicit focus on enabling the study and fostering of implicit cooperation. We achieve this through a novel methodological approach embedded within the framework: the enrichment of agents’ partial observations with system-level KPIs and the integration of these KPIs into a multi-objective reward function. This creates a unique feedback loop, demonstrating a viable pathway for guiding autonomous, self-interested agents towards collectively beneficial, coordinated behaviors without necessitating explicit communication or centralized control.
This work lays the foundation for future research enabled by the developed framework. The immediate next step is a comprehensive validation of the implicit cooperation mechanisms facilitated by this framework. This involves conducting large-scale MARL training experiments utilizing the framework’s full capabilities. Specifically, we will train agents using the implemented state-of-the-art MARL algorithms (i.e., PPO, APPO, and SAC) across the spectrum of training and inference paradigms: CTCE as a benchmark, the practical CTDE approach, and, most importantly, the fully decentralized DTDE paradigm that aligns with real-world LEM principles. These experiments will systematically evaluate how different market designs, grid conditions, and learning parameters influence the emergence and effectiveness of implicit coordination, quantifying the trade-offs between decentralization, performance, and stability.
Beyond this core validation, the modularity and extensibility of the framework open several promising avenues for future research:
•
Integrating more sophisticated DER models:
Enhancing the fidelity of agent models by incorporating more detailed representations of battery degradation, charging/discharging patterns of electric vehicles, building thermal dy namics, or heterogenous agent objectives (e.g., risk aversion, fairness concerns).
•
Exploring advanced MARL algorithms:
Implementing and benchmarking a wider suite of cutting-edge MARL algorithms, including those incorporating communication protocols (to contrast with implicit methods), alternative value decomposition techniques, or model-based approaches.
•
Scalability analysis:
Conducting a formal quantitative scalability analysis by executing simulations with increasing agent populations
( \mathsf { e . g . , \; \mathrm { { \scriptstyle { I O } } } } ,
50, 100+ agents) to plot computational time and analyze the impact of agent count on market KPIs.
• Application to real-world data: Validating and calibrating the simulation framework using empirical data from pilot LEM projects or real distribution networks to enhance its accuracy and practical relevance for policy analysis.
• Analysis of communication constraints: Extending the framework to explicitly model the impact of realistic communication network limitations (latency, bandwidth) and potential threats (e.g., false data injection) on the robustness and security of decentralized market operations.
We believe this LEM simulation framework will serve as a useful tool for the research community, policymakers, and industry practitioners striving to design, analyze, and deploy the intelligent, resilient, efficient, and truly decentralized energy systems required for a sustainable future.

H I G H L I G H T S
• Lean multi-agent DRL (L-MADRL) framework developed for networked microgrid energy management.
• Integrates DQN with single-level KKT-based reformulation of a bi-level problem.
• Explicit inclusion of ATC ensures secure and network-aware power exchanges.
• Achieves cost reductions of 10.3% (5- bus) and 2.6% (14-bus) for microgrids.
• Increases ER profits by up to 11.4% while maintaining runtimes under 3 s.
G R A P H I C A L A B S T R A C T
A R T I C L E I N F O
Keywords: Deep Q networks Energy management systems Uncertainty handling Stochastic optimization Risk management Microgrids
Abstract
This study introduces a Lean Multi-Agent Deep Reinforcement Learning (L-MADRL) framework for energy management of networked microgrids (NMGs) with multiple electricity retailers (ERs) and microgrids (MGs) under renewable and load uncertainties. Coordinating energy exchanges in such systems is challenging due to the need for market efficiency, technical feasibility, and scalability. The proposed framework combines a multi-agent Deep Q-Network (DQN) with a single-level reformulation of a bi-level optimization model. In this formulation, the upper level maximizes ER profits and the network’s available transfer capability (ATC), while the lower-level MG cost minimization is replaced by Karush–Kuhn–Tucker (KKT) conditions, yielding a mathematical program with equilibrium constraints (MPEC). This hybrid design offers two benefits: (i) technical constraints such as power flow limits, generator capacities, and market rules are embedded in the MPEC, freeing DRL agents from constraint enforcement and improving learning stability and policy reliability, and (ii) explicit ATC consideration enhances power transfer efficiency and enables network-aware coordination. Performance was evaluated on PJM 5-bus and IEEE 14-bus test systems against deterministic, risk-neutral (RNSO), and risk-averse (RASO) stochastic optimization. Results show that in the 5-bus case, L-MADRL reduced MG costs by 10.3% and increased ER profits by 3.7%, while in the 14-bus case costs decreased by 2.6% and profits rose by 11.4%. L-MADRL also improved ATC, exceeding the best benchmark by 32% in the 5-bus system and by 30% initially and 10% at peak in the 14-bus system. Across all cases, runtimes remained below 3 s, highlighting the framework’s scalability and computational efficiency.

1 . Introduction
Energy remains a cornerstone of economic development, and as global priorities shift toward sustainability and decarbonization, ensuring efficient, resilient, and reliable energy distribution has become a central concern for utilities, policymakers, and grid operators. In this context, microgrids which are localized energy systems capable of operating independently or in coordination with the main grid have gained prominence as a strategic pathway for modernizing the power sector [1]. Their ability to integrate renewable energy technologies (RETs), improve energy access, and foster grid resilience makes them key enablers in the transition from centralized fossil fuel based infrastructures to decentralized clean energy networks. Deterministic models remain the first analytical approach through which researchers have tried to minimize cost, enhance reliability and more recently improve environmental impacts in the energy management of microgrids. Wu et al. minimized the levelized cost of energy for a Malaysian PV–diesel–battery system, constraining loss-of-load probability (LOLP) to 5% and arriving at a diesel mix that still covers 99.5% of demand [1]. Where a full MILP formulation proved computationally heavy for the energy management of a standalone MG, Sedighizadeh et al.
splited the horizon into 24-h windows applying approximate dynamic programming and a bee-colony heuristic algorithm which slashed solver time by 75% with only a 2% cost gap [2]. For grid-tied systems, Khan et al. developed a day-ahead EMS around a hybrid electric-thermal storage with vehicle-to-grid services; even without uncertainty modelling their approach trimmed operating cost and
CO_{2}
emissions by 0.8% and 5.3% respectively [3]. Where MILP and MINLP formulations proved intractable, meta-heuristics have been adopted, albeit with no global optima guarantees. For instance, Roslan et al. employed a lightning-search algorithm (LSA) to schedule a diesel–PV–battery microgrid in real Malaysian load conditions, trimming grid import and operating cost by about 62% and cutting CO2 nearly 62%, all with far lower CPU burden than classical back-tracking or MILP methods [4].
A particularly transformative evolution of this type of energy system is the emergence of networked microgrids (NMGs), where multiple microgrids are interconnected through physical or virtual links and co-ordinated through shared control strategies or market mechanisms [5]. This interconnection facilitates enhanced operational flexibility, energy sharing, and the collective use of distributed energy resources (DERs). They also enable strategic islanding capabilities in the event of grid disturbances, supporting both grid resilience and energy autonomy, especially in vulnerable or remote regions. For example, Zhe et al. casted the distribution network (DN) as a Stackelberg leader that posts dynamic buy/sell tariffs, while prosumer MGs responded with unit commitment decisions. Solving the resulting bilevel MILP raised the DN revenue by 8% and clipped MG operating costs by 4% without breaching voltage limits [5]. Chen et al. treated five IEEE 33-bus microgrids as rational agents in a Shapley-value cooperative game where each MG posted a non-negative payoff and the total power purchase cost was reduced by 10% [6]. Merabet et al. explored a cluster of microgrids having diesel generators and solar PVs which shared a medium-voltage feeder offgrid; their results showed that coordinated power exchange trimmed fuel costs by 4.3% and paid back the feeder CAPEX in under four years [7].
While deterministic approaches remain quantitative baselines upon which advanced methods improve, they ignore forecast errors and the unpredictable behaviour of consumers with respect to their load demands. These uncertainties introduce volatility in power supply, complicate demand–supply balancing, and challenge both short-term scheduling and long-term investment planning. In networked configurations, such uncertainties can propagate across the system, affecting inter-microgrid coordination and leading to inefficient dispatch, suboptimal exchanges, or even reliability issues. These gaps pave the way for stochastic (SP), robust (RO) and Chance-Constrained (CCP) approaches, especially as they relate to NMGs. For instance, Nikmehr and Rasad’s Monte Carlo reliability analysis confirms that simply interconnecting MGs without any market layer cuts ENS by 70% and system average interruption frequency index (SAIFI) by 55% compared with islanded operation [8]. Seyednouri et al. compressed 200 wind/PV scenarios to 30 and embedded them in a price-setting bilevel MILP; their results showed that each MG operating cost fell by 7.5%, while the DISCO profit increased by 6.9%. Likewise, the loss-of-load risk dropped by 35%, and their sensitivity analysis revealed that supercapacitors below 0.2 p.u. of battery capacity risk jeopardizing all of the positive results obtained [9]. Jani et al. proposed a two stage stochastic optimization approach for the day-ahead and real-time energy management of microgrids; their work reduced the overall system costs by 5.5% and RES curtailment was also reduced by 15% [10]. Karimi et al. developed a multi-objective bilevel model that first maximizes the upper level distribution network operator’s (DNO) profit and then minimizes both the MG independence loss and its energy not served (ENS); their results revealed independence improved by 12% and the ENS dropped 63% without compromising on the profit realized by the DNO [11]. Similarly, Jani and Jadid proposed a two-stage bi-level framework in which a cooperative retail market clears day-ahead energy trades among networked MGs, while a real-time layer re-dispatches every few minutes to absorb renewable and load fluctuations; their results yielded operating cost reductions of $61 and an additional $44 when BESS is included in individual MGs [12]. Where scenario counts explode or tail events are prominent, some researchers have resulted to chance-constrained and robust optimization approaches. Aghdam et al. enforced a 5% violation probability on both emissions and power balance in their networked microgrid formulation. Their results showed that CO2 emissions dropped by 9.2% with a modest 1.3% increase in cost, and tightening epsilon 𝜖 from 10% to 1% increased cost by over 4% [13]. Gao et al. in their work allowed each MG to solve a local robust OPF with polyhedral uncertainty and exchange boundary flows with each other via ADMM; the algorithm converged in a dozen rounds, holding worst-case voltages within ± 3% and at only 1.2% extra cost [14]. To hedge both expected and worst-case costs in networked microgrids, Kim et al. fused a p-robust objective (p = 0.95) with a reduced scenario tree. Results revealed the expected operating cost reduced by 6.4%, while the worst-case cost fell by 12%, revealing a sweet spot between pure stochastic and pure robust formulations [15]. Wang et al. advanced the concept further for combined-cooling–heatingand-power (CCHP) MGs. They formulated a Wasserstein-based two-stage distributionally robust optimisation (WTSDRO) that treated wind power errors as ambiguity sets around the empirical distribution [16]. More recently, Bo et al. demonstrated that robust optimisation can operate at sub-hourly granularity: they embedded a budget-of-uncertainty layer inside a five-minute rolling MILP for an integrated-energy campus microgrid. Column-and-constraint generation solved each window in real time. Their approach reduced worst-case operating cost by about 10% while average cost rose only modestly; crucially, all hydrogen-pressure and thermal constraints remained feasible under every admissible PV/load realizations [17].
Accurate scheduling alone is insufficient if the upstream network lacks the capacity to accommodate the scheduled power transfers. Consequently, ATC emerges as a critical factor in effective energy management, particularly for utilities managing NMGs. ATC quantifies the remaining margin by which power can be transferred between different areas of a network without violating system constraints such as line limits, voltage boundaries, or reliability margins [18], and in the context of NMGs, ATC becomes a vital operational parameter for planning dayahead or intra-day transactions, and guiding real-time power exchange decisions. Liu et al. utilized a fully distributed Jacobi and Gauss–Seidel algorithms in computing the deterministic ATC across five areas [19]. Hou et al. showed that demand response itself is a latent ATC resource. By co-optimizing flexible loads, they were able to increase real-time network capacity, curtail RES losses, and still lower total cost [18]. Probabilistic studies by Wei et al. and Ávila-Ávila et al. reveal that 95% or 90% quantile ATC values are 12–15% below deterministic means, yet targeted network upgrades could help to increase these probabilistic ATC values further [20,21]. Complementing these, Wang et al. embedded ATC evaluation directly within market operations via a bi-level model; the upper level computed the ATC while the lower level handled the economic dispatch [22]. In addressing the multifaceted issues pertaining to uncertainties and ATC maximization, the use of SP, RO, and CCP comes with non-trivial limitations; SP relies on credible joint prob ability distributions of the stochastic parameters considered, in practice this necessitates large scenario trees accompanied by aggressive reductions, which could oftentimes attenuate tail events. This consequently inflates the complexity of bilevel MILP in NMG settings. CCP hinges on a user specified violation rate 𝜖 and tractable surrogates for joint chance constraints. RO avoids probability distributions but is highly sensitive to the choice of uncertainty set; polyhedral and budget sets frequently ignore temporal/spatial correlation, trading renewable utilization and ATC for conservatism, and may still under-hedge if misspecified. In addition, the high compute time needed by these conventional methods, particularly in regard to NMGs is enormous, and often-times not reliable for use in real-time environments.
In response to these challenges, reinforcement learning (RL), particularly deep reinforcement learning (DRL) has emerged as a promising solution. DRL combines the adaptive, sequential decision-making capabilities of RL with the function approximation strength of deep neural networks, enabling intelligent decision-making in dynamic, uncertain, and high dimensional environments. Unlike traditional optimization methods, DRL learns optimal control strategies through continuous interaction with the environment, adapting in real time as system conditions evolve. This makes DRL especially well-suited for solving energy management problems in complex NMG configurations. For instance, Yin et al. added “arousal” and “valence” variables to an actor–critic HVAC controller for a building in a standalone microgrid, so exploration escapes local optima; their results cut daily energy bills by 9% while keeping indoor temperature within ±0.5
𝑜
𝐶 [23]. Claessens et al. compressed 400 heterogeneous heat pump homes into one cluster-level DQN; after a month of simulation the agent reduced the electricity costs by 18% and shaves 0.9 MW (17%) off the evening peak [24]. Liu & Mao enrich the state of an actor–critic with one-hour PV and load forecast in a grid-tied single MG; the “information-enhanced” agent beats vanilla DDPG by 5.6 – 12.9% on cost while maintaining voltage inside ±5% [25]. Zhou et al. extended the idea to an electric-heat-gas microgrid where a continuous action DDPG co-optimizes battery and CHP, lowering daily costs by 6.8% with convergence in 300 episodes [26]. For networked microgrids, Tan et al. allowed each residential MG to train a Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) agent locally; the results of their approach reduced the average daily cost by 4.1% and training time by 38% [27]. Guo et al. approximated a Stackelberg equilibrium with a dual layer actor–critic; where the DSO was the price-setter, and the optimal dispatch was done by the MG agents. Equilibrium emerged within 250 episodes, boosting the DSO profit by 5% and reducing the MG costs by 4% [28]. Monfaredi et al. targeted an electric-thermal cluster in a grid-tied multi-energy MG by combining MADDPG with stacked denoising auto-encoders. When tested on an IEEE 33 bus and 8 node gas grid, costs fell by 9% and CO2 emissions fell by 8% [29]. Hedayatnia et al. decoupled training and execution, splitting an offline optimal EMS phase into an online DRL policy. Their results showed the MG cost dropped by 12.9% and run-time by 17% relative to a dueling-DQN baseline, while transmission losses reduced by 6% [30]. Gao et al. injected graph-attention and entropy annealing into Soft-Actor–Critic for a six MG cluster. The algorithm reduced operating costs by 10.2% and RES curtailment by 14.7% [31]. Wang et al. proposed a data-driven multi-agent stochastic-game RL for a networked microgrid with the goal of minimizing costs and improving grid stability [32]. Samadi et al. complemented these advances with a fully decentralized, multi-agent RL where self-interested DER and customer agents learn cost optimal bids via actor–critic algorithms, while an upper-level manager clears local electricity-and-heat trades without exposing raw data. Their results during testing finalized transactions in <2 s, increased the aggregator’s revenue by 5%, and reduced total MG costs by 7% [33]. Yang et al. deployed a Rainbow deep-RL controller that jointly scheduled a wind-farm battery and reserve purchases. By directly mapping forecasted wind and price trajectories to continuous charge/discharge actions, the agent absorbed forecast error automatically and increased the utility’s revenue in every simulated market scenario [34]. Foruzan et al. demonstrated that even a tabular multi-agent RL scheme where each generator, storage unit and customer learns autonomously can drive an islanded MG toward a Nash equilibrium dispatch that lowers fuel use and unmet load probability [35]. Vergara et al. extended RL to inverter-level services where a decentralized actor–critic scheme dispatches on each PV inverter every few seconds and converges to near optimal voltage regulation, limiting additional PV curtailment to <2.5% [36]. Zhou et al. combined deeplearning forecasts with a lightweight DDPG agent for battery scheduling in an integrated energy MG; the RL policy cuts solution time by 61% while sacrificing only 3.1% reductions in cost accuracy relative to an MILP, a trade-off that is crucial for real-time operation [26]. Going beyond electricity-only systems, Zhang et al. framed carbon-capture and power-to-gas dispatch as a Markov game and trained a prioritized experience replay Soft-Actor–Critic (SAC). They observed that when prediction errors exceeded 10%, their PER-SAC reduced total cost by approximately 11.6% [37].
The above discussions show that existing EMS frameworks for MGs and NMGs broadly fall into three methodological families. The first family comprises deterministic formulations and their extensions to stochastic, robust, or chance-constrained optimization. Deterministic EMS schemes for single MGs or simple MG clusters already achieve notable cost and emission reductions using MILP, MINLP, or metaheuristics [1–7]. Their main limitation is that they either neglect uncertainty entirely or only handle it through point forecasts, which can be particularly restrictive in networked settings where forecast errors propagate along the network and affect inter-microgrid exchanges. This has motivated scenario-based stochastic, chance-constrained, and robust formulations for NMGs that co-optimise local DERs, storage, and interconnection flows [8–17]. These approaches capture uncertainty more faithfully, but they typically lead to large-scale mixed-integer programs with many scenarios, long solve times, and they rarely treat ATC as a central objective. ATC-oriented works such as [18–22] focus on computing deterministic or probabilistic transfer margins, sometimes embedded in a market model, but are not usually integrated with detailed NMG EMS and multi-microgrid DRL policies. The second family emphasizes economic interaction and hierarchical decision-making. Here, the distribution network operator, a retailer, or an aggregator is modelled explicitly as a leader that sets prices or dispatch signals, while microgrids or prosumers act as followers that minimize their own operating costs [5,9,11,12,22]. These bi-level or game-theoretic structures capture market behaviour and decentralized decision-making, and some of them already incorporate ATC or line-flow constraints. However, they remain optimization-centric: each scheduling horizon still requires solving a large (often stochastic) bi-level MILP or MINLP, and technical limits are enforced purely through the solver. As a result, online scalability and real-time deployment remain challenging, especially when highdimensional uncertainties or many microgrids are involved. The third family uses deep reinforcement learning to mitigate repeated large-scale optimization and to handle high-dimensional, dynamic environments. DRL has been successfully demonstrated for single MGs, building-level demand response, and multi-energy clusters [23–26,34–37], and more recently for networked or multi-microgrid systems [27–33]. These works show that DRL can reduce cost, peak load, or emissions while greatly accelerating decision times compared with solving a full optimization problem at each step. Nevertheless, most of them either (i) do not embed a full ER–MG bi-level market structure with explicit KKT conditions for the follower MGs, or (ii) enforce network and generator constraints using penalty terms in the reward, which might leave some residual infeasibilities and complicate training.
In light of this, the present work combines elements of all three families. Structurally, it retains the economic clarity of bi-level models by formulating an upper layer that maximizes ER profits and network ATC and a lower layer that minimizes MG operating cost, then recasts the lower layer via its KKT conditions into a single-level MPEC with explicit network, generator, and storage constraints. Methodologically, it uses a lean multi-agent DRL (L-MADRL) framework to learn policies over this constrained environment, so that feasibility with respect to ATC and DER limits is enforced by the MPEC rather than by the DRL agents themselves. In contrast to pure optimization-based NMG frameworks

and pure DRL approaches [27,29–33], the proposed L-MADRL framework explicitly includes ATC in the upperlevel objective, models ER–MG coordination over a weakly meshed network, and learns policies that, once trained, achieve near real-time decision speeds while maintaining technical feasibility under renewable and load uncertainties. As later shown in Section 6, this yields consistent cost reductions for MGs and profit increases for ERs relative to deterministic, risk-neutral, and risk-averse stochastic benchmarks on the same PJM 5-bus and IEEE 14-bus systems, while improving ATC and keeping testing runtimes close to those of a deterministic baseline. Consequently, the main contributions of this work are as follows:
We formulate a bi-level optimization problem in which an upper layer coordinates multiple grid-connected energy resources (ERs) and a lower layer manages interconnected MGs; ERs and MGs exchange power over a weakly meshed distribution network with explicit network constraints. The bi-level problem is then recast as a mathematical program with equilibrium constraints (MPEC) by replacing the lower-level problem with its Karush–Kuhn–Tucker (KKT) conditions, yielding a tractable single-level model.
Thereafter, we implement a microgrid coordinator/controller that jointly oversees ER–MG interactions; upper-level objectives are to maximize all ERs profit and maximize the ATC between sources (ERs) and sinks (MGs), while the lower level minimizes MGs operating cost.
We then develop a L-MADRL framework to solve the resulting MPEC under solar, wind, and load-demand uncertainties on both the ER and MG sides.

2 . Deep reinforcement learning (DRL)
Developing an effective RL model is rarely a straightforward task; the performance of the final solution depends heavily on the design choices, algorithmic sophistication, and careful tuning throughout the training process. Traditional Q-learning is constrained to discrete state and action spaces, limiting its applicability to many real-world scenarios. In contrast, energy management problems in microgrids often involve continuous state and action spaces, necessitating more advanced approaches such as DRL.
Among the suite of DRL techniques, DQN stands out as one of the most widely adopted and adaptable algorithms. By combining deep neural networks with RL’s sequential decision-making framework, DQNs are capable of learning powerful policies and approximating Q-values for all actions across a given state space. This makes them a strong candidate for tackling high-dimensional and complex control tasks.
2.1 . Deep Q-networks (DQN)
Deep Q-Networks (DQNs) are a form of reinforcement learning that use neural networks to approximate the Q-value function. They represent a significant advancement over conventional Q-learning by enabling scalability to high-dimensional input spaces and supporting continuous state representations. In situations where the true Q-value function cannot be computed explicitly due to the size of the state-action space, DQNs approximate it using a neural network parameterized by weights 𝜃 denoted as
Q ( s , a ; \theta )
. The network is trained to minimize the temporal difference (TD) error [38], guiding the model toward optimal value estimation over time. Fig. 1 shows the inner workflows of the DQN algorithm.

The epsilon parameter, initially set high to encourage exploration, is gradually decreased as training progresses, allowing the algorithm to increasingly rely on its learned policies to find optimal solutions.
3 . Problem formulation
The bi-level problem formulation for the NMGs is presented in subsequent sections; the upper level objectives and constraints are first pre-sented for the ERs, and the lower level formulates the objectives and constraints for the MGs. The networked microgrid controller/coordinator (MGC) coordinates the operations of the entire system in a centralized EMS scheme.

• Dual feasibility: This represents the non-negativity of the dual multipliers.
• Complementary slackness: This links the primal and dual variables.

4 . Lean multi-agent DRL (L-MADRL framework)
The proposed L-MADRL framework aligns with the principles of safe DRL where the conventional burden of satisfying a wide array of technical, operational, and network-level constraints is decoupled from the learning process itself. In classical DRL setups for energy systems, the agent is expected to simultaneously learn optimal actions while navigating complex feasibility regions defined by system dynamics, power flow constraints, generator limits, and interconnection rules. This dual responsibility often leads to unstable learning, infeasible actions, and slow convergence, particularly in high-dimensional stochastic environments.
To address this, L-MADRL adopts a modular architecture in which constraint handling is delegated to a dedicated and analytically tractable optimization layer. This layer is derived from a reformulated single-level optimization problem based on the KKT conditions of the original bilevel structure, ensuring that every action proposed by the DRL agents is inherently feasible with respect to network and market constraints. This design relieves the agents from the computational overhead of constraint checking and can instead focus exclusively on learning optimal policies for managing stochastic variables such as solar irradiance, wind speed, and load demand in order to maximize long-term rewards under these uncertainties. Consequently, the learning process becomes more stable and computationally efficient, since the agents are relieved of the burden of navigating complex feasibility regions during training. Additionally, the proposed structure guarantees that technical and economic constraints are rigorously satisfied throughout system operation, thereby enhancing the reliability and safety of the decision-making process.
The proposed algorithm implementation relies primarily on two tenets: the DQN algorithm used by each agent, and the MPEC reformulation of the original bilevel problem shown in Eq. (86) with the detailed process depicted in Fig. 2. It is pertinent to note that each agent depending on the stochastic parameter being assigned to it and the corresponding node on the network receives its own set of observations (states) as shown in Fig. 3. Using these inputs, each agent receives its own local state(s) in parallel and takes an action from its corresponding action set (discussed in subsequent sections). These action sets represent real constant values by which the agent adjusts its predicted wind, solar, or load parameter to closely match its actual value.

4.1 . Training process
As a precursor to the training phase, historical data for the load demand, wind speed, and solar irradiation were obtained from the data repositories by
^ { [ 4 1 , 4 2 ] }
, and [43] respectively for the years 2007 – 2010. These data after being extracted and tidied were split into two sets: set 1 contained the data records for 2007 – 2009, while set 2 contained the records for 2010.
Using set 1, we first constructed synthetic forecasts by perturbing the measured series with random errors whose distributions were chosen to reflect the characteristics of each stochastic variable: for the load; additive errors were sampled from a Gaussian distribution, for the solar irradiation, errors were sampled from a Beta distribution, for the wind speed, errors were sampled from a Weibull distribution. For each stochastic parameter and each hour of the day, the deviations between these synthetic predictions and the actual values over 2007–2009 were collected. The empirical mean and standard deviation of these forecast errors at each hour were then computed and included as state inputs to the DRL agent, as described in Fig. 3.
In training the DRL model in Fig. 3, the data in set 2 (year 2010) was utilized, however, we randomly extracted exclusively the 24-h data for the 15th of July 2010 for testing, hence our data points comprised 8736 data points. As before, we again generated the predicted profiles by perturbing the actual 2010 series with random samples drawn from the fitted distributions. In this way, the agent learns under statistically realistic forecast errors, while keeping the NMG EMS formulation agnostic to the particular forecasting technique. In practice, any forecasting algorithm could be used to produce the predicted values and associated error statistics required by the proposed L-MADRL framework. Integrating a more advanced forecasting module is therefore straightforward and would not require changes to the L-MADRL framework design. Although actor–critic algorithms such as SAC, A3C and PPO are popular for continuous control, we deliberately adopt a value based Deep Q Network (DQN) for the proposed EMS because it matches the structure and computational constraints of our problem. The agents do not output generic continuous controls, but select one multiplier from a finite catalogue of discrete error factors that scale the forecast error standard deviation of each stochastic parameter, which yields a large yet finite combinatorial action space that is naturally handled by DQN, whereas a continuous policy would still need to be projected back to the nearest admissible multiplier, breaking the assumptions of policy gradient updates and introducing additional approximation errors. Moreover, every environment step requires solving the single level MPEC with the transformed stochastic parameters to compute the feasibility penalties
R _ { 2 } ,
so off-policy data reuse is crucial; on-policy methods such as SAC, A3C and PPO would demand many more fresh trajectories and therefore many more expensive MPEC solves, while DQN uses a replay buffer that allows extensive reuse of past transitions. In addition, the reward landscape induced by deviation and penalty terms can be highly non smooth, so policy gradient methods may suffer from noisy and unstable gradients unless heavily regularized, whereas value based DQN learns Q values from temporal difference targets without differentiating through the environment, which typically yields lower variance targets and makes training less sensitive to hyperparameters such as learning rate and entropy regularization. Finally, DQN provides simple and transparent exploration control through an epsilon greedy policy, which is easy to tune in the presence of large negative rewards for infeasible or highly suboptimal schedules, while entropy regularization in SAC or PPO can encourage overly aggressive exploration in regions that consistently produce infeasible operating points, which is undesirable given the high cost of each environment evaluation.
4.2 . Testing process
The testing phase is as described in Fig. 4. Here, given the day-ahead predictions of the stochastic parameters (load, solar, and wind) from the ERs and MGs, the hourly mean and standard deviation from the historical data (2007–2009), these inputs are fed into the commensurately trained agent(s).
The agent(s) then perform the transformations internally, and sends these transformed values as inputs to the deterministic bi-level NMG framework from where the optimal schedules and objectives are derived. The testing process all happens on a timescale of milli-seconds when compared with the time required for uncertainty handling with the stochastic optimization methods showcased as benchmarks in this work. It is critical to note here that a larger network does not necessarily translate to a proportionate increase in the number of DRL agents in the L-MADRL framework. While it is true that ERs and MG operators are modelled by different agents, each agent is designed to handle multiple nodes that share the same type of stochastic parameter (for example, wind at ERs, wind at MGs, solar at
\mathbf { M G s } ,
or load at MGs). In other words, the number of agents scales with the number of distinct uncertainty types, not with the number of buses. Hence, when the system size increases, what grows is primarily the action space of some agents, not the agent count itself. Alternatively, for scalability and faster learning, the action space because of the larger network could be partitioned across two or more agents that each cover a subset of nodes. This was precisely what was done for agents 4 and 5 in the 14-bus case which handled the load demand uncertainty, since nine (9) buses had load attached, they were split between two agents; agent 4 handled five of the nine load buses and agent 5 handled the remaining four. Either way, both design choices remain compatible with our L-MADRL framework.
5 . Two-stage stochastic optimization
This section describes the procedures involved in implementing the two-stage risk-neutral and the risk-averse stochastic optimization with CVaR. The uncertainty modeling technique used is described first alongside the scenario generation/reduction process.
5.1 . Uncertainty modelling
Accurately modeling the uncertainties of stochastic parameters by considering only deterministic forecasts is too risky, and could lead to sub-optimal schedules especially when planning to participate in a dayahead or real-time electricity market. To circumvent this, MCS could be utilized in generating multiple plausible scenarios of these variable parameters in the next hour, or next day as the case may be. This process is the ’scenario generation’ phase and it relies on using accurate PDFs that closely fits the stochastic parameters. In this work, the normal distribution was used to model the stochasticity of the load demand, while the beta and weibull distributions were used to model that of the solar irradiance and wind speed respectively.

Where
\mu _ { \mathrm { l o a d } }
and

6 . Case study
Two different sub-transmission grid networks were utilized as case studies to test the L-MADRL framework alongside the deterministic, risk-neutral, and risk-averse two-stage stochastic optimization methods being used as benchmarks. The framework was written in Python (version 3.10.16) using important modules such as PyTorch for the multi-agent DRL part and MIP for the single-level MPEC solution. The developed L-MADRL framework was trained and tested on an AMD Ryzen 9 5950x 16-core processor equipped with an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4070 Ti Super GPU. Subsequent sections reveal these case studies in more detail and discuss the results obtained.
6.1 . Case 1: PJM 5 bus network
As the first case study, a modified PJM 5 bus network is utilized, this simplified test grid is used to test the energy management prowess of the L-MADRL in a networked MG setting with uncertainties present. Table A1 in Appendix A shows the technical and economic parameters of the ERs and MGs connected to different nodes in the network and Fig. 7 shows the schematic of the network alongside the different DERs attached to the respective nodes.
The learning trajectory for the three agents in the 5-bus case network is shown in Fig. 6. The solid lines represent the rolling mean of the agent’s learning progress after 100 episodes until the end of training. At the onset, At the onset, each agent explores the environment more due to the epsilon-greedy action selection policy defined in Eq. (94) for each period. The overall trend observed is an increase in the normalized rewards across all agents evidenced by the sharp improvement in the first 200–300 episodes. In particular, the agent (agent 3) responsible for the MG load demand stochasticity’s reached a reward of 0.9 at about the 1500th episode and remained close to 1.0 for the rest of the training horizon. The MG solar and wind agent (agent 2) experienced a bit of delay but largely followed a similar pattern to agent 3 achieving rewards asymptotically close to 1.0 after about the 3000th episode. The wind ER agent (agent 1) displayed the most visible non-monotonic behaviour. After an initial increase, it experienced a temporary degradation in the reward around the 1000th episode before recovering and converging to a high reward of around 0.95. The dip suggests the difficulty in learning the stochasticity’s of the wind speed in the ER nodes possibly due to the variance observed in the training data, however, since at each episode, the agent still has the ability to explore its environment, it eventually learns to choose more optimal policies.

6.2 . Case 2: IEEE 14 bus network

For the 14-bus system in Fig. 15, all five agents start with very low normalized rewards close to zero and experience a steep improvement during the first 300–400 episodes. In this early phase, the curves are relatively spread and the instantaneous rewards exhibit noticeable variability, which is typical of intensive exploration. As training proceeds, the rewards of all agents increase monotonically and rapidly cross 0.8, indicating that the agents are already learning beneficial coordinated behaviors. Between roughly 500 and 1000 episodes, the slopes of the curves gradually flatten and the agents approach their steady-state rewards. The wind-based ER agent (agent 1) is marginally slower but also reaches a high reward level close to 1.0. After about 2500 episodes, all five trajectories become almost flat and tightly grouped near 1.0, and the variance of the instantaneous reward signals is significantly reduced.

7 . Conclusion and future work
This study proposed a lean multi-agent deep reinforcement learning framework for the energy management of NMGs under uncertainties. Initially, the NMG problem was represented as a two-layer energy management problem where the upper layer handled the objectives and technical constraints of all the ERs, and the lower layer represented the objectives and technical constraints of the MGs. In order to solve this dual-layer problem under uncertainty and obtain globally optimal solutions, the lower level problem formulations were represented by its equivalent KKT conditions. The resulting KKT equations were then added as additional constraints to the upper level problem hence transforming it into a MPEC (single-level) problem for the NMGs. Since conventional methods that handle uncertainties in complex systems of this nature face challenges such as dependencies on scenarios, and overly conservative solutions, a L-MADRL was proposed to draw on the strength of DQNs through multi-agents and the resulting MPEC problem formulation. The beauty of this framework lies in its relinquishing the burden of technical feasibility to the single-level formulation whilst focusing solely on learning optimal policies for all stochastic parameters (solar irradiance, wind speed, and load demand) considered. These proposed methodology bench-marked against the deterministic, two-stage RNSO, and two-stage RASO cases were tested on two distinct case networks; PJM 5 Bus and IEEE 14 Bus. The results of the L-MADRL performed better when compared to the other benchmarks, simultaneously minimizing the overall costs of the MGs and maximizing the total profits of the ERs and the ATC of the test grid. Also, the time taken by the L-MADRL to handle the complexity of these networks with uncertainties for the 5 and 14 bus system were less than 3 secs, while it took far more time when any of the other three benchmarks were utilized. In a future work, a more decentralized EMS using L-MADRL framework would be explored where the privacy concerns of each and every market player/entity is considered accordingly.

Deep reinforcement learning-based multi-objective energy management system for microgrids under flexible energy market
DOI: 10.1016/j.apenergy.2025.127223

Jingxuan Wu
∗
iD
, Shuting Li, Yun Yu, Yajuan Guan, Baoze Wei, Zhe Chen
Aalborg University, Pontoppidanstraede 111, Aalborg, 9220, Denmark
H I G H L I G H T S
• A novel online energy management strategy independent of massive historical datasets.
• Multi-objective intelligent decision-making agent using a deep reinforcement-learning algorithm.
• An online energy market evaluation method for electricity trading guidance in flexible energy markets.
• High-resolution operations to handle transient oscillations in the power flow and energy balance.
A R T I C L E I N F O
Keywords: Energy Management Energy Storage System Microgrid Power Flow Control Reinforcement Learning
Abstract
The promotion of renewable energy in Microgrids (MGs) brings uncertainty from weather and climate change, thereby challenging the energy management systems (EMSs) in energy allocation tasks. This paper proposes a reinforcement learning (RL)-based online EMS (RLEMS) approach to solve the multi-objective optimization of power flow in an MG with a high proportion of uncertainty. A novel online energy management framework is proposed in the RLEMS, which utilizes the information extraction ability of RL algorithms to map the multi-dimensional MG states with optimal power flow operations, diluting the time sequence self-correlation in solving uncertainty. Different from conventional time series optimization methods, the proposed RLEMS can be deployed with few-shot historical datasets and operate the MG with a high resolution. The global economic horizon of the RLEMS is established through a novel energy price evaluation model (EPEM) instead of conventional prediction approaches, in which the vague evaluation of electricity price is quantified and projected to the RLEMS timescale and the MG scope. The multi-timescale uncertainty and multi-dimensional MG status are combined with distinguished priorities by the EPEM and RLEMS reward function. The performance of the proposed RLEMS is validated through realistic numerical experiments. The proposed RLEMS can maintain the stable and economical operation of the MG for over 240 hours continuously with only 24-hour training data. The comparison with cutting-edge approaches indicates that the proposed RLEMS provides promising cost-saving performance.
1 . Introduction
Renewable energy has been developing rapidly in the last decades due to public awareness of environment-friendly energy structures, leading to the growing implementation of wind and solar generation. Microgrids (MGs) are essential units to interface distributed generators into power systems and therefore the terminal system, which suffers from the uncertainty and intermittence of renewable energy [1]. To improve the power balance and power efficiency of MGs, energy storage (ES) systems and cooperated energy management systems (EMSs) are deployed to dispatch the local energy spatiotemporally.
An energy management system (EMS) is defined as a tertiary-level control system to monitor, dispatch, and optimize the MG system [2]. The internal power and energy balance is an important optimization target for EMSs in MGs, which affects the frequency and voltage stability of the AC bus [3]. EMSs optimize the power flow by operating the ES systems and controllable loads according to the system dynamics [4]. Many automatic control methods have been introduced into EMS applications to enhance the power balance of MG systems. In [5], fuzzy logic is deployed to switch the operation modes of an MG. The dispatched distributed generators include a fuel cell, a battery, a photovoltaic (PV) system, and the utility grid. Model predictive control (MPC)
