is introduced in [6,7] to realize the distributed power flow control in a multi-MG system. The robustness of the system is enhanced through this approach. Benefiting from the development of communication technology, the Internet of Things (IoT) is attracting increasing attention and bringing feasibility for centralized EMS in MGs. In [8], an IoT-based intelligent EMS is implemented in a PV-battery building to achieve the internal energy balance and net-zero emissions. However, the increasing proportion of solar or wind energy in modern power systems brings uncertainty to the energy market, long-term energy balance as well as local power flow, requiring long-term energy allocation strategies to optimize the MG from an economic aspect [9].
The economic operation of MG is another essential optimization target of EMSs [10]. In traditional EMSs, the dispatching tasks of MGs are reformulated as optimization problems. By employing prediction techniques to address uncertainty, mathematical optimization algorithms are introduced to determine the step-ahead schedule results for the MG [11]. Mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) is a common algorithm in EMS. In [12], the charging and discharging events of a battery are scheduled by the MILP in an MG to reduce the operation cost. In MG with discrete control objectives like electric vehicles or controllable loads, MILP demonstrates high performance in renewable energy dispatching [13]. For multi-objective optimization problems, the reformulated system incorporates additional nonlinear elements that necessitate heuristic algorithms for precise resolution [14]. Particle swarm optimization (PSO) is a typical heuristic algorithm in EMS applications [15]. In [16], PSO is deployed to realize the day-ahead EMS for a microgrid with a high proportion of PV generation. In [17], PSO is utilized to cooperate with an artificial neural network in an EMS for islanded MGs. Other algorithms, like teaching-learning, can also effectively solve the optimization problem in MG systems, and the calculation efficiency can be improved through novel quantum computation [18]. However, the uncertainty introduced by renewable energy or user actions is not solved directly in traditional optimization-based approaches. The economic performance of these methods is highly dependent on the prediction accuracy of loads and renewable generation. Even though the deep learning (DL) algorithm has significantly enhanced the forecasting precision in EMS applications, there still exists a conflict between the horizon of the EMS and the accuracy degradation of prediction methods [19].
Online EMS approaches enhance independence from highperformance prediction methods by treating energy management as a decision-making problem. Reinforcement learning (RL) is an effective algorithm for EMS in MGs with a high proportion of uncertainty [20]. Different from conventional offline EMS, which requires external forecasting methods, RL can solve the time series problem with internal deep neural networks [21]. Existing research has implemented plenty of RL algorithms in EMS applications, including Q-learning [22], Deep Q-network (DQN) [23], Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG) [24], Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) [25], Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) [26,27], etc. A comparison among RL approaches and conventional methods is presented in Table 1. RL outperforms traditional methods in solving multi-objective problems and considering more complex systems. However, among all the existing methods, solutions to uncertainty always require numerous historical local databases. Time sequence problems are resolved by recurrent neural network blocks, typically long-short-term memory, in external prediction components or internal DL networks. These approaches expand input data in the time domain, on the one hand, increasing the computational burden of the training process, and on the other hand, raising the deployment cost in data preparation work and weakening the adaptability towards environmental and system configuration changes.
To release the historical data dependency of the EMS approaches and take the operation precision into account simultaneously. A novel RL-based EMS (RLEMS) is proposed in this paper, which on one hand, realizes the multi-objective power flow optimization in an MG with a high proportion of renewable energy, on the other hand, eliminates the computation burden caused by increased operation resolution. The contributions of this work are summarized as follows.
A novel RLEMS framework that concentrates on mapping the multi-dimensional system states and optimal power flow operations is proposed instead of the conventional time series arrangement approaches, diluting the time sequence self-correlation of uncertainty. The RLEMS utilizes the information extraction capabilities of DDPG algorithms to operate the power flow against uncertainty from weather, users, and markets without extra pre-diction components, releasing dependency on long-term historical training datasets, decreasing the deployment cost while enhancing the operation precision.
An energy price evaluation model (EPEM) is proposed to expand the dimensions and range of injected data, improving the information extraction efficiency and ensuring that the proposed RLEMS can work with limited historical data. This model-based online function projects global market uncertainty to the online RLEMS time scale according to the MG configurations. On one hand, the EPEM releases the computation burden caused by increasing resolution; on the other hand, the EPEM provides a novel evaluation method that jointly considers the uncertainty and device constraints.
A resilient MG topology is designed to interface with the RLEMS, ensuring the continuous and stable operations of the RLEMS for MGs. The ultra-capacitor (UC) is utilized as an energy buffer, and the RLEMS is softly interfaced into the grid converter, avoiding the conflicts between tertiary RLEMS and primary controller, enhancing the system’s power balance with rapid power oscillation.
The rest of the paper is organized as follows. The architecture of the MG and the topology of the RLEMS are presented in Section 2. In Section 3, the mathematical definition of the proposed EPEM is pre-sented and analyzed. The structure of the RL agent and DDPG algorithm is studied in Section 4. The numerical experiment is implemented for the proposed RLEMS, and the results are presented and analyzed in Section 5. At last, a conclusion is drawn in Section 6.

2 . The topology of the proposed RLEMS and MG
MGs are essential units in modern power systems to integrate dis tributed generators. Most sustainable generation sources, for instance, PV systems, batteries, fuel cells, and UC, are naturally DC sources, while AC loads dominate the demand side. Hence, a DC bus is implemented to integrate the power suppliers as shown in Fig. 1. The utility grid, connected to the DC bus via a DC-AC converter, and the battery, interfaced through a bidirectional boost converter, are regulated by the RLEMS. The PV system is deployed via a maximum power point tracking (MPPT)-regulated boost converter. Residential loads consume power from the AC bus through an inverter. The bidirectional converter for UC maintains the DC bus voltage with a droop logic to guarantee the power balance on the DC bus. In this sense, the UC provides the dynamic energy buffer to mitigate transient power oscillations and inertia for energy dispatching, enhancing the resilience of the MG system.
In the proposed MG architecture, the uncertainty is injected through multiple aspects. The PV system injects uncertainty from local weather. The residential loads are affected by stochastic user actions. The flexible energy price is determined by the global weather, climate, and supply–demand relationship. The renewable generation

In this MG system, data from sensors with different collection frequencies are reorganized into several resolutions by rolling window averaging and interpolation in the IoT database. The RLEMS accesses the minute-resolution data series. The normally distributed data errors caused by communication latency or measurement issues are filtered through the data reorganization process.

The RL agent is updated continuously according to the online reward. In this sense, the multi-objective optimization problem of the MG system is reformulated as an online power flow control framework.
3 . The proposed energy price evaluation model
Long-term optimization and real-time operation are considered separately in most existing EMS approaches, leading to information asymmetry and cooperation issues among different EMS layers. Existing research relies on prediction methods [28], stochastic models [29], or fuzzy logicbased evaluation to handle uncertainty from the weather and market sides. However, within the continuous operation in an MG, online corrections for evaluation results or thresholds are always necessary for deployment. Considering the dynamic states and flexible power operations during the continuous workflow, an EPEM is designed as a guide for economical operation to establish a long-term horizon in high-resolution online EMS. The EPEM consists of a dynamic energy price evaluation and an MG system status evaluation.

4.3 . Reinforcement learning algorithm
A DDPG framework with four deep neural networks—two actor and two critic networks—is used for the RL algorithm. The deep neural network structures are presented in Fig. 3.
The actor deep neural network takes observations as input and expands the hidden layer through two fully connected (FC) and Rectified Linear Unit (ReLU) layers. The critic deep neural network has two inputs: the observation is expanded through an FC-ReLU layer and regulated to the same dimension as the expanded action by an FC layer. The two scenarios include two extreme phenomena that represent the short-supply and over-supply situations. The winter case emphasizes the energy trading between the local MG and the utility grid. Since the PV generation could hardly cover the power demand. In the summer case, the RLEMS focuses on the daily renewable energy allocation, and the energy market has minimal influence on the optimal operation of the MG.
The MG is operated by the same RLEMS in the two scenarios, and the DDPG algorithm is trained with 24-hour data and validated in 10-day scenarios. In continuous operations, the trained agent can self-adjust against seasons, weather, loads, and market changes, since these factors usually evolve gradually and smoothly at minute resolutions. The retraining process actually initializes the RLEMS agent based on the training dataset. The transferability of the proposed RLEMS is considered through improving the deployment efficiency. Compared to conventional EMS methods, the retraining and deployment work of the proposed RLEMS is efficient and timely, providing considerable transferability for the proposed RLEMS. In this sense, the DDPG agent for each season is trained independently, considering that the two scenarios are not continuous.

5.2 . Ablation experimental validation
To illustrate the performance of the DDPG algorithm, a PPO algorithm is also designed as a comparison. The hyperparameters of the two algorithms are presented in Table 3. The definition of empirical parameters in the reward function is further discussed in the Appendix. Both RL algorithms are implemented in the environment equipped with the proposed EPEM and the same reward function, indicating similar optimal operation logic. DDPG and PPO agents are actor-critic RL algorithms, differing primarily in their exploration strategies and output formats. DDPG explores the environment by an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck noise model and outputs a constant, and the PPO algorithm uses a Gaussian noise model and provides a random number expressed by its mean and standard deviation.
The training process of the DDPG and PPO agents is shown in Fig. 6. The blue curve represents the DDPG agent and the red one represents the PPO. Both agents stabilize within 200 episodes and explore the economical operation logic in the following episodes. The oscillation during the training process is affected by the exploration algorithm and DL network structures. The DDPG algorithm can provide a stable reward during the training, but the critic network is suffering from dramatic oscillations. Compared to the PPO algorithm, the exploration range of the DDPG algorithm is limited and might not reach an extremely high reward. However, the actor network of the DDPG agent can converge to the optimal reward more easily than the PPO algorithm in these two scenarios.

5.3 . Comparative experiments
The economic performance of the proposed RLEMS is further verified by comparing it with existing methods in real-world applications: PSO-based day-ahead EMS, LP-MPC online EMS, and grid-connected MG without ES. In this paper, prediction results with distinct accuracy, 100 %, and 80 %, will be fed to the PSO algorithm to consider the complete performance range of traditional EMS. LP-MPC will be fed with ideal prediction results, where the LP is applied for dayahead optimization, and MPC focuses on system stability with a 10-step look-ahead.
The total energy expenses with different methods are shown in Fig. 10. The daily energy cost is presented in Table 4. The proposed RLEMS cannot achieve the lowest daily expense compared with existing approaches. However, the total energy expense is the lowest. The reason for this phenomenon can be explained by two perspectives: 1) The proposed RLEMS works with dynamic horizons defined by online system states. Hence, RLEMS do not outperform existing methods within each daily case. 2) The proposed RLEMS is not within the framework of traditional EMS approaches. The different decision logic leads to unique operation points, resulting in oscillations and disturbances in short-term economic evaluation. In this sense, the economic cost is evaluated by long-term expense.
For PSO-based day-ahead EMS, the horizon is fixed and discrete, making the EMS unable to react to system dynamics and transient uncertainty. Besides, the performance of the PSO-based approach degrades as the prediction accuracy decreases. The LP-MPC approach, as a typical multi-layer EMS framework, effectively compensates for the dynamic oscillations during online workflow. However, the fixed horizons of the upper layers and online controllers are still facing challenges in information updating and layer interactions. On the contrary, the proposed RLEMS is independent of the prediction methods, and the proposed EPEM provides the long-term horizon for the RLEMS, making the RLEMS intelligent and stable enough to cope with complex system status. The operation logic defined by the proposed EPEM, together with the reward function, is verified economically in Fig. 10. Compared with common real-world applications, the proposed RLEMS achieves a 10.2 % cost-saving in the winter case and 33 % in the summer case.

6 . Conclusions
A multi-objective RLEMS is proposed in this paper to realize the intelligent real-time power flow control in a converter-interfaced MG. The main works can be summarized as follows.
A novel online RLEMS framework is proposed to realize the multi-objective optimization of MGs with a high proportion of uncertainty. The RLEMS decouples the multi-dimensional system states with the optimal power flow operations with few-shot datasets through a DDPG algorithm, further decreasing the deployment cost and enhancing the feasibility of centralized EMS.
An innovative EPEM is designed to provide online economic evaluations, transferring global market uncertainty to the RLEMS timescale and MG scope. Based on the proposed EPEM, the uncertainty, the system power balance, and the economic cost are jointly considered in one reward function with distinguished priorities.
Comprehensive validations are conducted to verify the performance and superiority of the proposed RLEMS. The ablation study indicates that the optimal operation logic defined by the proposed EPEM, together with the reward function, is economical and stable for the MG. The performance of the proposed RLEMS is validated by comparing it with existing methods and applications. The results demonstrate that the proposed RLEMS can ensure the stable operation of the MG system and obtain a 10.2 % to 33 % cost-saving in the economic aspect.
The RLEMS provides a novel framework to establish low datadependency EMS systems, further promoting the potential application of cutting-edge AI models in energy technologies. In future research, the generalization of the proposed approach to different MG configurations will be explored, and forefront AI models will be deployed within this framework through transfer learning and few-shot learning technologies.

Meta-reinforcement learning for multi-energy building microgrids: Curriculum design, rapid adaptation, and scalable deployment
DOI: 10.1016/j.enconman.2026.121652

Research paper
Sai Sasidhar Punyam Rajendran ∗, Alemayehu Gebremedhin
Department of Manufacturing and Civil Engineering, Norwegian University of Science and Technology, Teknologivegen 22, Gjøvik, 2815, Norway
A R T I C L E I N F O
Keywords: Building microgrids Multi-energy systems Reinforcement learning Meta-learning Adaptive energy management Curriculum learning
Abstract
Multi-energy building microgrids meeting local demands is a promising solution for sustainable and self-sufficient energy communities. However, consumption diversity across heterogeneous buildings creates a deployment bottleneck that requires an adaptive and scalable energy-management strategy. A novel metareinforcement learning framework was proposed in this study that integrates an enhanced reptile-based meta-learning algorithm with Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) to learn a generalized policy capable of rapid building-specific personalization. Two curriculum learning approaches were applied to assess the impact of task organization on meta-learning outcomes, focusing on seasonal variations and building diversity. Rigorous hyperparameter optimization was performed to identify high-performance models (three per curriculum) for comprehensive deployment analysis.
The trained meta-policies were deployed on five unseen test buildings across four seasons. The adapted policies achieved a mean reward improvement of 23.9% over the trained meta-policy, with constraint violations reducing by 38% and daily operating costs decreasing by 12.2%, statistically validated through a Wilcoxon signed-rank test
( \mathsf { p } = 1 . 1 1 \times 1 0 ^ { - 2 0 } )
. Curriculum-2 (progressive building diversity) outperformed Curriculum-1 (seasonal progression) by 53% in mean adaptation improvement, demonstrating that learning building heterogeneity is more valuable than mastering seasonal patterns for adaptive energy management. Future research directions include hardware-in-the-loop validation, adaptive curricula, and multi-agent coordination for community-scale deployment.
1. Introduction
Relying on the traditional centralized grid infrastructure is challenging because the ever-increasing energy demand requires upscaling of the grid and adding additional generation sources. Energy stakeholders introduced microgrids, distributed energy resources installed close to the demand points to meet the demand locally, thereby reducing the strain on the primary grid [1]. However, designing multi-energy microgrids that can efficiently meet electrical, heating, cooling, and transportationdemand is challenging because of high installation cost, intermittent renewable generation, complex energy coupling, and diverse energy consumption characteristics [2].
Multi-energy microgrids operate at different scales from individual buildings and residential communities to large industrial complexes. Residential buildings account for approximately 30% of global energy consumption and 27% of greenhouse gas emissions to meet electrical, heating, and cooling demands [3]. Hence, the substantial carbon footprint in the residential energy sector represents a critical challenge for sustainability efforts. However, there is also a tremendous opportunity by transforming residential buildings into energy-independent entities through building-level microgrids, reducing the dependence on centralized infrastructure while improving resilience and sustainability [4, 5].
Energy-independent communities leverage local renewable generation (primarily rooftop PV), energy storage systems, and intelligent energy management to minimize grid interactions and maximize self-consumption. The concept extends beyond mere self-sufficiency to encompass broader goals of sustainability, resilience, and economic efficiency [5]. When considering cold countries, approximately 65%–75% of residential energy consumption is heating. However, with multi-energy microgrids can achieve significantly higher self-sufficiency and efficiency than single-vector approaches. The coupling between electrical and heating networks creates system flexibility to convert the excess electricity into heat to store and use it later to offset heating energy needs [6].

1.1. Literature review
Multi-energy microgrid design has three stages: planning, energy management and control, and deployment. Energy management focuses on optimizing the energy resources available to meet the demand reliably and efficiently [2]. Energy management involves designing a framework that optimizes a target objective subjected to system constraints such as operation limits, energy balance, energy storage dynamics, and ramp-up/ramp-down limits [7,8].
Traditional microgrid optimization has relied on mixed-integer linear programming (MILP), dynamic programming, and meta-heuristic algorithms, with MILP providing optimal solutions when problems are accurately formulated with known parameters [9]. However, these methods struggle becasue of non-linear behaviors arising from battery efficiency, heat pump performance (COP), and CHP operation significantly.
Although genetic algorithms and other metaheuristic approaches can handle non-linear and multi-objective formulations, they require extensive function evaluations leading to high computational costs and limiting real-time applications. Moreover, the algorithms generate static solutions based on forecasted conditions rather than adapting to evolving situations [7]. These limitations are particularly more pronounced in residential microgrids, where building demand patterns exhibit high variability and diversity making the forecasting accuracy more error prone and challenging to optimize.
Reinforcement Learning (RL) and Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) approaches have been adopted for microgrid energy management due to its ability to adapt to complex and dynamic environments [7,10]. These methods enable agents to learn optimal policies directly from environmental interactions without requiring explicit system models or precise prior knowledge of system dynamics [11,12]. Through trial-and-error learning, RL algorithms continuously refine strategies and adapt to changing microgrid conditions and market dynamics [13]. DRL further enhances these capabilities by integrating deep neural networks to process high-dimensional data and learn complex patterns for improved decision-making. Once trained, RL policies can make rapid real-time decisions and develop robust policies that perform well across varying operating conditions [10].
A comprehensive systematic review by [14] highlights the role of deep neural networks in managing distributed energy sources while emphasizing the need for trustworthy AI solutions that ensure explainability, robustness, and fairness in critical infrastructure applications. Authors in [15] developed a risk-aware deep reinforcement learning approach to optimize energy prices in demand response programs, achieving 30% cost reduction and 32% emissions reduction. Multi-agent Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG) was integrated with LSTM forecasting in [16] to optimize pricing and battery usage and manage uncertainties in smart grids, enhancing system stability through reduced peak-to-average ratios. Authors in [17] proposed a physically consistent neural network (PCNN)-assisted Hierarchical Model Predictive Control framework for grid-interactive residential buildings to ensure fair compensation, achieving up to 37.8% energy cost reduction and 82.1% improved grid service performance while maintaining end-user comfort.
Researchers in [18] developed a multi-agent reinforcement learning framework with Self-Adaptive Random Exploration (SARE) for distributed automatic generation control, demonstrating enhanced frequency stability in systems with high renewable penetration. Extending these concepts to networked environments, authors in [19] proposed a two-stage multi-agent deep reinforcement learning approach combining Optimal Energy Management System (OEMS) with Dynamic Real-Time Operation (DRTOP), effectively managing 300-600kW consumption patterns across multiple microgrids while minimizing operating costs and handling operational uncertainties through dynamic pricing mechanisms.
Authors in [20] developed a transfer learning framework to scale DRL controllers across different buildings, achieving 10% cost reduction and 10%–40% fewer temperature violations. In contrast, the study in [21] proposed model-based reinforcement learning for improved sample efficiency in microgrid operations. However, standard reinforcement learning approaches still face significant challenges in residential applications due to diverse energy consumption, making it difficult to find the optimal policy working across all buildings without significant re-training [22].
In this light, meta-learning addresses these limitations by enabling models to learn a generalized policy and rapidly adapting policies to specific building characteristics with minimal additional data [23]. Meta-reinforcement learning has been applied in various applications such as control strategies [24], load frequency control [25–28], service restoration [29], resilience [30], forecasting models [31,32], stochastic power-dispatch [33,33] and energy management [34–38]. Some of the popular meta-reinforcement learning algorithms used are Reptile [39], first-oder MAML (FOMAML) [30], LSTM-based model [36], MAML [31, 38] and in-case of multi-agent systems the commonly used algorithms were deep meta-deterministic policy gradient (DMDPG) [25,26,34,40].
Authors in [35] proposed a two-level Evolutionary Multi-Agent Deep Meta-Actor-Critic (EMA-DMAC) framework for load frequency control, improving convergence and robustness while enabling rapid adaptation across multi-area microgrids. Similarly, the study [24] applied meta-learning with Deep Q-Networks for battery, creating autonomous agents that optimize operations across diverse scenarios with minimal training data. The deployment advantages become particularly evident in [38], where Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning (MAML) enables rapid optimal policy generation during early microgrid operation stagesreducing the data requirements and operational costs through quick adaptation. Authors in [41] further demonstrated metalearning’s superiority with a framework outperforming traditional RL by 20%–50% while providing interpretability through Shapley Value analysis, enabling rapid online adaptation after offline multi-task training.
Researchers in [39] focused on the temporal adaptability in home energy management, using auto-encoders to detect seasonal context shifts and adapt policies accordingly. However, the single-building focus limits exploration of building diversity. These studies collectively demonstrate meta-learning’s ability to create easily deployable, rapidly adaptable energy management systems that generalize across diverse operational environments with minimal site-specific training.
1.2. Contributions
Based on the literature, considerable attention has been dedicated to buildingenergy management , as shown in Table 1. However, a significant gap exists for large-scale community-level deployment. Four key areas that need further analysis are
• limited adaptation and scalability across diverse building energy characteristics
• poor training efficiency and high data requirements for buildingspecific deployment
• insufficient integration of multi-energy coupling dynamics
• simplified reward design lacking multi-objective representation
Hence, the primary research objective in this study is to develop a novel meta-reinforcement learning framework for building multi-energy microgrid management that coordinates electrical and thermal systems through heat pump integration. Through meta-policy training with adaptation, the framework rapidly adapts to diverse building characteristics using minimal data, improving sample and training efficiency. In contrast, traditional RL methods require extensive perbuilding training, making deployment across building communities computationally prohibitive for practical applications. The framework employs curriculum learning with progressive complexity to achieve robust performance across diverse buildings and seasonal conditions. The key contributions of this study are as follows:
• Developed a meta-learning framework for multi-energy building microgrids that rapidly adapts to diverse buildings with minimal data.
• Enhanced the Reptile algorithm with adaptive gradient aggregation to improve meta-policy generalization across diverse building profiles.
• Designed integrated management for coupled heating-electrical systems (heat pumps, batteries, PV) balancing multiple objectives.
• Implemented curriculum learning with progressive complexity and conducted hyperparameter optimization to identify optimal architectures for model deployment.
• Deployed trained meta-policy (generalized-policy) on unseen buildings for a personalized/adapted policy.
The proposed framework fundamentally changes how building microgrids join energy communities. By learning transferable representations of multi-energy dynamics across diverse buildings, new buildings can join an energy community as active prosumers with minimal deployment overhead, eliminating the retraining burden and data requirement that limits the scalability of conventional energy management approaches.
2. Methodology
The Fig. 1 shows the meta-reinforcement learning framework designed for the adaptive energy management of multi-energy building microgrids. Each building’s energy system characteristics are considered a distinct task in the meta-learning task distribution. During training, the system samples diverse building tasks and trains a metapolicy to learn generalizable energy management strategies. The inner loop adapts to building tasks by modeling energy components (demand, capacity, multi-energy systems) and receiving performance rewards. In contrast, the outer loop updates the meta-policy based on experience across multiple buildings. This dual-loop architecture enables the system to learn efficient energy management rather than memorizing building-specific patterns, discussed more in Section 2.1.
The curriculum scheduler ensures the model is exposed to diverse seasonal patterns, staging task sampling across different times of year to capture varying heating and energy demands. The meta-iteration checkpoint monitors whether the meta-policy achieves stable performance across these diverse conditions. The framework can rapidly deploy and adapt the learned meta-policy to new buildings without extensive retraining, effectively handling heterogeneous consumption patterns while maintaining computational efficiency.
2.1. Meta-reinforcement learning
Meta-reinforcement learning (meta-RL) aims to learn reinforcement learning algorithms through machine learning rather than human engineering. While traditional RL learns a policy presented in Appendix, meta-RL learns the algorithm 𝑓 that produces the policy. This approach shifts human effort from direct algorithm design to developing training environments and parameterizations needed for data-driven algorithm learning [23].
Meta-RL employs a two-level architecture: an inner-loop performs adaptation to the specific buildings, and an outer-loop that learns to adapt quickly. Typically, these tasks share state space  and action space  but differ in reward function

3. Multi-energy building microgrid
A cold climatic region, such as Norway, was considered as the case study owing to the seasonal variations and significant mismatch between energy generation and demand. The energy demand dataset designed by the authors in [42] by collecting smart meter data from 99 buildings in the Tronødelag neighborhood was used. The authors applied k-means clustering to the hourly consumption data to identify four distinct load profile groups (A-D), representing buildings with similar consumption patterns. However, demand data was normalized for data security purpose and the hourly demand is multiplied by a scaling factor given by Eq. (2), where the total demand was estimated from the source [43]. The energy demand dataset was segregated into electrical and heating demand using k-means clustering based on the correlation between outdoor temperature and high energy demand, as discussed in detail in [44]. Fig. 2 shows the electrical and heating demand profiles of five households for one year. This section presents the comprehensive design of the reinforcement learning environment (inner-loop of meta-RL) for multi-energy building microgrid management, detailing the component modeling, state–action formulation, and reward structure that enables effective policy learning.

This comprehensive design ensures learned policies maintain acceptable performance across all operational objectives, reflecting the complex nature of microgrid optimization.
4. Meta-learning framework
Meta-reinforcement learning for building microgrid energy management requires a fundamentally different approach compared to traditional single-task reinforcement learning. The workflow consists of three essential components: diverse task generation, meta-learning framework, and model adaptation, which are discussed in the following sections.
4.1. Data engineering for meta-learning task
An effective meta-learning framework for adaptive energy management relies on the design of a diverse distribution of related, but distinct, tasks. Each task represents a building with unique consumption patterns, preferences, and configuration. This diversity enables the model to learn generalizable adaptation strategies.
The task distribution pipeline shown in Fig. 3 transforms Norwegian building energy data into a meta-learning distribution dataset for building energy management. Buildings were configured with heterogeneous parameters: capacities of energy components, battery storage parameters, and heat pump specifications, creating diversity with unique state spaces and objectives. This diversity provides implicit guidance about promising approaches for different building types, reducing trial-and-error time by focusing on strategies likely to succeed. The training also prepares the system for variability in consumption patterns, equipment efficiency, and behavioral preferences rather than assuming idealized conditions.
4.1.1. Curriculum learning
Applying meta-reinforcement learning to multi-energy building microgrid management presents unique challenges. Traditional approaches that expose the meta-learning agent to the full complexity of the problem space from the outset often result in unstable training dynamics and high variance in adaptation performance. This instability is particularly pronounced in the current research settings because of the heterogeneity across buildings and drastic seasonal variations, causing a generation-demand mismatch.
Seasonal variation has been a critical challenge in building microgrid energy management. Winter heating demands follow inverse patterns with solar generation availability, requiring fundamentally different optimal policies across seasons. A straightforward approach is to use the complete annual cycles before meta-policy updates. However, that increases computational burdens with extremely slow learning progress and does not leverage the inherent problem structure to learn daily & weekend consumption and seasonal patterns from limited but efficient data.
To address these challenges, a structured curriculum learning approach was designed to progressively increase building diversity and seasonal variations . The curriculum design is motivated by the principle of compositional complexity, which states that complex behaviors can be more effectively learned by first mastering simpler component skills [40].
In this study, two contrasting curriculum approaches were designed to investigate optimal training strategies for meta-RL. Curriculum-1 (Table 2) employed a 7-stage seasonal progression, beginning with summer-only scenarios for 450 iterations before gradually introducing spring, autumn, and winter conditions, while simultaneously expanding the building pool from 15 to 60. The days-per-season parameter decreased from 8 to 2 across stages, ensuring that the horizon was constant for the entire training.
Conversely, Curriculum-2 (Table 3) implements a simple 3-stage approach with all four seasons present from the outset (fixed seven days each per season), focusing solely on building complexity progression from the easiest 20 to all 60 buildings. During the training period, a stochastic sampling method was used to expose the meta-learner to each training building in multiple seasonal contexts, weather conditions, and operational scenarios. This extensive sampling combined with disjoint validation ensures learned adaptation mechanisms generalize to unseen building characteristics rather than memorizing specific training patterns. The specific stage lengths and season/day selections were determined empirically through preliminary training runs, guided by observed meta-learning dynamics including gradient stability and performance progression across stages.
The rationale behind selecting these two approaches was to test whether meta-learning benefits from gradual seasonal complexity (curriculum-1) or full seasonal exposure with progressive building diversity (curriculum-2). Curriculum-1 allows incremental development of season-specific policies, potentially enabling better feature reuse, while Curriculum-2’s constant seasonal exposure may yield more robust policies at the cost of slower training.
The approach transforms the high-variance and unstable training into structured learning with lower variance and superior generalization. The curriculum manager, as shown in Fig. 3, samples the meta-task batch with the corresponding building energy system characteristics that the framework uses in the next stage for training and finding the optimal generalized meta-policy.

5.1. Hyperparameter tuning
Reinforcement learning agents learn from evolving policy-generated data, creating extreme sensitivity to hyperparameter choices through compounding feedback loops. In energy management applications, high variance in reward signals across seasonal patterns and building behaviors amplifies this sensitivity, making precise hyperparameter optimization essential for stable convergence. In addition, meta-reinforcement learning algorithms introduce additional complexity through hierarchical optimization, where inner-loop hyperparameters control taskspecific adaptation to individual buildings. Conversely, outer-loop hyperparameters govern meta-learning for general policy improvement. This dual optimization creates complex interactions where hyperparameter choices at each level profoundly influence model performance and generalization capabilities.

Although shallow networks provide rapid adaptation owing to fewer parameters, they may lack the representational power to capture complex energy management patterns across diverse building types. In contrast, deeper architectures offer hierarchical feature extraction, where early layers can learn general energy dynamics and deeper layers specialize in management decisions, risking slower adaptation and potential overfitting to the meta-training distribution.
The activation function choices (ReLU, ELU, tanh) further control the learning dynamics of the network, with the sparsity of ReLU promoting faster adaptation and smooth gradients of ELU potentially improving the meta-gradient. Hence, the architectural decisions and outer-loop hyperparameters collectively determine the ability of metapolicy to serve as a practical initialization point for rapid buildingspecific adaptation while maintaining sufficient generality across the heterogeneous energy management domain.

5.3. Model adaptation
The trained generalized meta-policy was deployed on unseen buildings to learn building-specific energy management characteristics through a limited number of adaptation episodes. To determine an appropriate episode count, a systematic evaluation was conducted using two representative meta-learning models: sage (Curriculum-1) and dashing_bee (Curriculum-2). Each model was tested on 5 diverse households across winter and summer to capture contrasting operational conditions. The meta-policy was first evaluated without adaptation to establish the baseline performance, and then fine-tuned using 𝑁 (varied from 2.5 to 20 episodes) adaptation episodes of household-specific data. After each adaptation, the resulting policy was evaluated for three episodes to measure the performance improvement and adaptation efficiency (defined as the percentage improvement per episode).
Fig. 8(a) shows a clear positive relationship between adaptation episodes and performance improvement. Sage achieves improvements ranging from 2.7% (at 2.5 episodes) to 20.7% (at 20 episodes), while dashing_bee demonstrates stronger adaptation capability with improvements from 5.4% to 48.6% over the same range. Fig. 8(b) reveals that adaptation efficiency peaks at seven episodes for both models; however, the five-episode case achieves 95% of this peak efficiency, indicating diminishing returns beyond this point.
Hence, five adaptation episodes were selected for the deployment analysis as they balance strong adaptation quality with computational efficiency. The six trained meta-policies were then adapted to five buildings completely unseen during the meta-training phase, with each building sampled for one week per season, yielding 28 days of operational data across the four seasons. The meta-policy and adapted policy performances were compared across all deployment conditions to assess both the impact of curriculum design and the effectiveness of the adaptation process.
Fig. 9 shows the distribution of policy performance across six operational metrics, comparing the meta and adapted policies for both the curricula. The adaptation produced consistent improvements across multiple objectives, with Curriculum-1 models achieving a mean reward improvement of 17.7% and Curriculum-2 models achieving 30.0%. The episode reward distributions shifted toward less negative values after adaptation, with Curriculum-2 exhibiting a tighter and more symmetric adapted distribution than Curriculum-1, indicating more predictable adaptation outcomes across unseen buildings.
The adapted policies demonstrated meaningful improvements, with total constraint violations decreasing by 33% for Curriculum-1 and 43% for Curriculum-2 after adaptation, while daily operating costs reduced by 8.0% and 17.4%, respectively. Moreover, Curriculum-2 meta-policy starts with fewer violations and lower energy shortage than Curriculum-1 even before adaptation, indicating that the curriculum design improves not only adaptation outcomes but also the quality of generalization.

This represents an economically rational strategy in which the agent prioritizes reliable energy delivery over renewable maximization when the two objectives conflict.
Across all six metrics, Curriculum-2 adapted distributions were more concentrated than Curriculum-1, with Curriculum-2 models achieving 53% higher mean adaptation improvement than Curriculum-1. This performance gap suggests that constant exposure to building diversity during meta-training produces a more robust initialization for building-specific adaptation than the seasonal progression approach adopted in Curriculum-1.
Fig. 10 shows the episode reward improvement distribution across four seasons for both curricula. Curriculum-2 outperforms Curriculum-1 in every season, most notably in spring (+29.1% and +13.6%) and summer (+36.0% and +21.0%), where higher PV availability and moderate heating demand provide the adapted policy with greater operational flexibility. Autumn shows strong and consistent gains for both curricula (Curriculum-1: +24.8%, Curriculum-2: +35.7%). Winter shows the lowest improvement (Curriculum-1: +11.5%, Curriculum-2: +19.3%), which is expected given the limited PV generation and peak heating demand that constrain the achievable improvement margins. Despite the lower reward gains, winter achieved the largest violation reduction (44%), indicating that the adapted policy prioritizes constraint adherence over reward maximization under the most demanding operational conditions.

5.3.1. Deployment considerations
The proposed framework primarily uses a simulation environment, and deploying it directly in a grid without additional validation is risky and expensive. Hence, Hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) acts as a crucial safety buffer between software simulation and real-world deployment, ensuring that the control algorithms are validated under real-time and hardware constraints before dealing with actual grid integration [55]. Software-in-the-Loop (SIL) tests if the control algorithm can execute on target hardware, establishing computational feasibility. Controller Hardware-in-the-Loop(CHIL) ensures the controller can operate within the desired time through communication protocols. Power Hardwarein-the-Loop (PHIL) testing incorporates equipment and validates the controller’s response to power dynamics and transients [55].
HIL testing provides valuable insights by systematically introducing constraints such as sensor noise, network communication delays, and hardware limitations. Moreover, control algorithms that excel under simulation conditions may struggle during communication latencies, limited processing power, or incomplete state information during critical control decisions. The most widely used HIL platforms are OPAL-RT [56], dSPACE, MATLAB/Simulink-RT, NovaCor RTDS [57], and Hypersim [58]. HIL platforms also provide environments for analyzing system vulnerabilities, such as component failures [56] and cyber-attacks [58] that cannot be practically tested on microgrids.
The rapid adaptation capability of the meta-RL framework requiring only five episodes is particularly valuable in HIL frameworks where testing time directly translates to higher costs and slower deployment. Moreover, the lightweight and enhanced Reptile meta-RL algorithm further reduces the computational requirements. In addition, online learning ensures the controller learns through the accumulated operational data, thereby providing advantages over static optimization approaches. The HIL framework could also showcase the communitylevel scalability of meta-RL application, where new building microgrids could be integrated into the network, and the system can adapt quickly without requiring complete system retraining or reconfiguration.
5.4. Limitations & future directions
The research scope was intentionally bounded by computational tractability and available resources, resulting in certain limitations that are discussed below alongside corresponding future research directions.
5.4.1. Reward design
The proposed reward function adopts a multi-objective formulation, balancing short-term priorities — operating costs, system stability, and renewable utilization — against long-term battery health/storage optimization objectives. However, coordinating multiple building microgrids with high PV penetration introduces grid stress risks, as simultaneous peak generation across buildings can result in excessive aggregate export that the local grid may not manage. Therefore, future studies can focus on developing an advanced reward structure that incorporates time-varying export penalties to mitigate grid stress without compromising building self-sufficiency or inducing unnecessary curtailment.
Reward weight selection presents a fundamental challenge in multi-objective reinforcement learning. However, identifying optimal weights requires extensive experimentation that may not generalize across diverse building types in meta-learning. This study used fixed weights after a preliminary exploration (Fig. 5) to balance the energy costs, comfort violations, and renewable utilization. Future work could explore evolutionary algorithms or multi-objective Bayesian optimization for automated weight-tuning. However, this introduces substantial computational overhead, and the trade-off between reward engineering effort and performance gains remains an open challenge in reinforcement and meta-learning.

Reward weights were kept uniform across all training buildings to ensure stable meta-gradient aggregation during Reptile updates. In contrast, heterogeneous reward compositions across buildings may introduce conflicting update directions, destabilizing the meta-policy rather than converging to a robust shared initialization. Extending the formulation to user-defined reward preferences through reward-conditioned meta-RL, where weights are provided as task context inputs, represents a promising future direction.
5.4.2. Curriculum engineering
One intriguing research finding was the influence of curriculum engineering on meta-learning effectiveness. The current curriculum design follows a fixed difficulty progression; however, an adaptive design that adjusts task complexity based on training performance metrics could further improve model performance. The design could consider a performance-triggered progression threshold to allocate sufficient training time in a potentially challenging phase, thereby improving training and deployment efficiency.
5.4.3. Framework applicability
Although validated on Norwegian building energy data, the framework is designed for global applicability with minimal architectural modifications. The core algorithm remains unchanged, requiring only region-specific design of state/action spaces, reward coefficients, and task distributions. The meta-learning foundation further enables rapid onboarding of new buildings, alleviating the deployment bottleneck without extensive retraining. Therefore, the framework supports scalable global adoption through region-specific parameter tuning rather than fundamental algorithmic redesign. Additionally, systematic benchmarking against building-specific analytical baselines (MPC, MILP) remains valuable future work to quantify the performance trade-offs between learned generalization and tailored optimization. The pipeline can be further improved by integrating attention mechanisms for capturing temporal and seasonal dependencies, Graph Neural Networks for modeling complex building interrelations, and probabilistic architectures to improve robustness and deployment credibility.
5.4.4. Peer-to-peer energy trading
Peer-to-peer energy trading represents an interesting pathway to address the grid stress (or weak grid) problem discussed in Section 5.4.1, enabling excess PV generation to be redistributed among buildings before grid export. Multi-agent reinforcement learning provides a natural coordination framework as an extension, where the trained meta-RL policies serve as competent base agents, avoiding retraining from scratch and enabling sample-efficient community-scale coordination. However, establishing a fair trading market that balances individual building preferences with collective community goals while ensuring transparency and end-user privacy remains a significant open challenge.

The proposed framework establishes a foundation for a transformative vision of networks of self-sufficient buildings that collectively form resilient, sustainable, and energy-independent communities. The authors plan to extend the framework, as discussed in detail in [59], toward integrating meta-RL and MARL for coordinated peer-to-peer energy trading and enabling the transition to self-sufficient energy communities.. A single meta-policy that can be deployed across multiple buildings in the community, each adapting to local characteristics while benefiting from collective learning through multi-agent coordination. Although the results demonstrate feasibility, the full potential of metalearning in revolutionizing building energy management remains to be unlocked through collaborative research efforts that address these challenges and opportunities.
6. Conclusion
The primary objective of this study was to propose a comprehensive meta-reinforcement learning framework for the adaptive energy management of multi-energy building microgridbalancing electrical and heating loads. The framework integratesan enhanced reptile-based meta-learning algorithm and proximal policy optimization PPO to find a generalized policy for diverse buildings, capable of rapid personalization, improving the sample efficiency and ease of deployment. Two curriculum approaches were developed and compared: Curriculum-1 modeled progressive seasonal complexity, while Curriculum-2 focused on progressive building diversity with constant seasonal exposure. Extensive hyperparameter tuning revealed that models with deeper architectures and the hyperparameter combination significantly impacted learning and adaptation capabilities.
Six high-performing models (3 per curriculum) from the hyperparameter tuning were deployed on five test buildings. The adapted policies achieved a mean reward improvement of 23.9% over the trained meta-policy, with total constraint violations decreasing by 38% and daily operating costs by 12.2%. Curriculum-2 outperformed Curriculum-1 by 53% in terms of mean adaptation improvement and exhibited superior consistency (coefficient of variation < 0.91). The adaptation benefit was statistically confirmed (Wilcoxon W=7162,
\mathtt { p = 1 . 1 1 \times } 1 0 ^ { - 2 0 } )
, with Curriculum-2 outperforming Curriculum-1 across all seasons (19.3% to 36.0%), and winter achieving the largest violation reduction (44%) despite the lowest reward gains. These results demonstrate that learning to build heterogeneity through progressive diversity exposure is more valuable for generalization than sequentially mastering seasonal patterns. The adapted policies showed increased grid dependency as a trade-off for reduced electrical shortages and constraint violations, reflecting an economically rational strategy that prioritizes reliability.

Appendix. Reinforcement learning
Reinforcement learning develops agents that learn optimal decision policies through environmental interaction. In this framework, agents take actions, observe state changes, and receive rewards, learning to maximize cumulative rewards by identifying optimal actions in various states. This approach excels in sequential decision-making problems like energy management in microgrids.
Formally, reinforcement learning operates within Markov decision processes (MDPs), defined as
\mathcal { M } = \left\langle S , \mathcal { A } , P , P _ { 0 } , R , \gamma , T \right\rangle
, where  is the state space,  the action space,
P ( s _ { t + 1 } | s _ { t } , a _ { t } )
the transition probability function,
P _ { 0 } ( s _ { 0 } )
the initial state distribution,
R ( s _ { t } , a _ { t } )
the reward function, 𝛾 the discount factor, and 𝑇 the time horizon. A policy
\pi ( a | s )
maps states to action probabilities. The probability of a trajectory under policy 𝜋 is:
P ( \tau ) = P _ { 0 } ( s _ { 0 } ) \prod _ { t = 0 } ^ { T } \pi ( a _ { t } | s _ { t } ) P ( s _ { t + 1 } | s _ { t } , a _ { t } ) ,\tag{A.1}
The trajectory
\tau = \{ s _ { t } , a _ { t } , r _ { t } , s _ { t + 1 } \} _ { t = 0 } ^ { T }
represents collected data during an episode. The RL objective is to maximize expected discounted return:
J ( \pi ) = \mathbb { E } _ { \tau \sim P ( \tau ) } \left[ \sum _ { t = 0 } ^ { T } \gamma ^ { t } r _ { t } \right]\tag{A.2}
With collected data
\boldsymbol { \mathcal { D } } = \{ \tau ^ { h } \} _ { h = 0 } ^ { H }
from multiple episodes, an RL algorithm functions as
f ( { \cal D } ) \; : \; ( ( \stackrel { n } { S \times { \cal A } } \times \mathbb { R } ) ^ { T } ) ^ { H } \; \rightarrow \; \varPhi
, mapping data to parameterized policies with parameters
\phi \in \varPhi .
Training often employs exploratory intermediate policies rather than purely greedy approaches.

Abstract
With the diversification of building functions and the popularization of electric vehicles, the difficulty in the operation and regulation of community microgrids that integrate renewable energy and energy storage systems has increased significantly. This study integrates real data, public datasets, and a scenario-based data generation framework for charging piles to construct a virtual community-level microgrid system. To increase the number of effective samples in reinforcement learning training, a semantic masking mechanism with environmental perception capability is introduced to achieve real-time optimal regulation of the microgrid under dynamic electricity price scenarios. The study conducted a systematic analysis under three action stepsize settings and a 30-day hourly optimization scenario, integrating multiple baseline models with multidimensional evaluation metrics. The results indicate that the generated charging pile power data accurately reflects both the consistency of group charging behavior and individual variation characteristics. Compared to baseline models, the Semantic mask DQN policy achieves an average reduction of 1.21%-3.73% in total electricity consumption, while simultaneously realizing operational cost savings of 1.76%-5.86%. This strategy effectively enhances the training stability of reinforcement learning models and significantly reduces the frequency of boundary triggers in energy storage systems. Under this framework, microgrids have enhanced their ability to cope with short-term power outage scenarios. The findings of this study provide intelligent optimization approaches and theoretical support for the efficient and low-carbon operation of building cluster microgrids with charging regions.
Keywords:
Building cluster microgrids, Semantic mask, Reinforcement learning, Charging pile, Real-time operational optimization
1.Introduction
1.1 Background
According to data from the World Meteorological Organization (WMO), the global average temperature has risen by 1.2°C over the past decade [1]. Addressing climate change, reducing greenhouse gas emissions, and ensuring sustainable energy supply have become the core drivers propelling a major transformation in the global energy sector [2]. With the continuous growth of social development and electricity demand, traditional fossil fuel power plants are increasingly struggling to meet the rising energy requirements. Expanding existing power grid systems not only requires massive investment but also entails additional greenhouse gas emissions, posing dual economic and environmental challenges [3]. In contrast, the application of renewable energy sources such as distributed photovoltaic (PV) power generation offers multiple advantages. Not only does it help reduce transmission losses and enhance grid reliability, but it also contributes to increasing grid resilience [4].
The trend toward electrification in transportation is gaining increasing attention, directly driving the widespread adoption of electric vehicles (EVs) [5]. Research indicates that by 2030, China's EV fleet is projected to reach 102 million units [6]. The development of infrastructure such as EV charging stations is precisely the key prerequisite for the large-scale adoption of EVs [7]. With the accelerated advancement of urbanization and the electrification of transportation, the energy consumption structure of various building complexes is becoming increasingly diverse, and real-time demand fluctuations are growing more pronounced. The large-scale integration of distributed PV power generation systems, charging stations, and energy storage systems is transforming traditional building complexes into localized energy communities capable of producing, storing, and consuming energy [8, 9]. The development of community-level microgrids can increase the utilization of renewable energy to a certain extent, reduce operational costs, enhance energy efficiency, and promote local economic development [10]. However, the increasing penetration of distributed PV systems, the rapid growth of EV charging demand, and the diverse energy profiles of multi-type buildings have also introduced significant challenges to local energy management. These developments have intensified shortterm fluctuations, increased operational uncertainty, and strengthened the coupling among PV generation, building demand, and EV charging behaviors. As these challenges become more pronounced, ensuring stable and reliable operation requires not only continuous upgrades to grid infrastructure, but also the integration of advanced management strategies and energy storage technologies [11]
1.2 Literature Review
Driven by carbon neutrality goals, the traditional centralized grid architecture reliant on fossil fuel power generation is accelerating its transition toward a distributed architecture that integrates renewable energy, energy storage technologies, and optimized energy management [12]. The Chinese government has set a clear goal of achieving carbon neutrality by 2060 and plans to deploy a cumulative total of 1,200 GW of solar PV and wind power capacity by 2030 [13]. In densely populated urban areas, PV is a more reliable clean energy source due to limited available space [14]. The application of rooftop PV systems is expected to reduce global temperatures by 0.05–0.13°C [15]. However, the uncertainty and intermittency of PV power generation make it impossible to meet the demand for stable electricity supply [16, 17]. Energy storage systems utilize fluctuations in electricity prices to enable charging and discharging, effectively addressing the challenges posed by the intermittent supply of PV power [18]. Integrating distributed energy systems with effective energy management in existing buildings can significantly enhance energy efficiency and flexibility [8].
This study reviews recent relevant research, as shown in the Table 1. Overall, photovoltaics and energy storage have become key components of energy management research. Meanwhile, as EVs become increasingly widespread and accepted, EV charging loads have become an indispensable component of community energy systems. According to statistics, by the end of 2022, the number of public charging stations for EVs worldwide had reached 2.7 million [19]. Most existing studies achieve the prediction or generation of real-time charging data for electric vehicles through methods such as typical parameters, probability density functions (PDF), and Monte Carlo simulations [20-22]. However, fixed EV charging modes overlook the uncertainty of actual user choices. Moreover, the daily travel distances of different vehicle types are not entirely identical [23]. This may affect its actual charging demand and frequency, and be reflected in the real-time load demand of the charging station. Selecting EV charging modes by fully considering user behaviors and types, while integrating multiple influencing factors, represents a modeling approach that better aligns with practical dispatch requirements[24, 25]. For certain actual charging piles load demand data, it aggregates the total electricity consumption of different users, thereby indirectly reflecting user charging behavior across different time periods. This study will utilize real-world datasets to model this behavior, generating real-time energy demand sequences for charging piles to serve as a portion of the total load.

Efficient optimization strategy is an important prerequisite for achieving the economical and stable operation of energy system. Swarm search algorithms have become an important approach to addressing this issue. Shoaib Ahmed et al. [32], focused on residential microgrids in Egypt, adopted an energy architecture integrating photovoltaics, wind energy, hybrid energy storage, V2H, grid connection and reduced the cost by a maximum of 2.91% through the Transient Search (TS) algorithm combined with time-of-use electricity pricing. Sankar Natarajan et al. [33], targeting large-scale commercial buildings, applied the Multi-objective Whale Optimization Algorithm (MOWOA) in similar energy systems and achieved a maximum reduction of 57.9% in electricity purchase costs. An advanced hybrid framework integrating a One-to-One-Based Optimizer, K-means clustering, and artificial neural networks (ANN) effectively achieves multiple optimizations in microgrid energy management, including operational costs, carbon emissions, and real-time responsiveness [38]. Moreover, due to its ability to interact with the environment and learn autonomously, DRL is employed to address problems in complex scenarios. Liu et al. [34], proposed a learning-based adaptive model predictive control enhanced by reinforcement learning (LearnAMR). In the energy system composed of photovoltaics, energy storage, and power grids, they further considered the impact of thermal inertia, reduced energy consumption by 12.1%, and achieved cost savings. In the fields of smart building constructions that prioritize indoor environments, energy efficiency, and economic costs, as well as smart city development integrated with computer vision, deep reinforcement learning (DRL) has demonstrated significant practical value [39, 40]. However, the training stability and convergence efficiency of DRL still face challenges. Action masking enables the selection of safe actions from the original action space [41]. Reducing the action space to include only feasible actions can also save training time [42]. This approach has significantly optimized the performance of DRL in other tasks [43, 44]. The frequent occurrence of natural disasters and extreme events has further exacerbated grid instability and the risk of power outages [45]. This will not only result in massive economic losses but also severely impact critical infrastructure. Distributed energy systems can effectively reduce dependence on external power grids. Therefore, while ensuring the stable and economical operation of the energy system, the strategy must maintain a certain level of available energy reserves to address short-term power outages.
Data driven approaches rely more heavily on hidden connections between variables while lacking the ability to assess real-time scenarios, reducing their interpretability and training stability. Semantic rules may serve as an effective approach to address this issue. Some studies have attempted to incorporate semantic rule inference models to tackle the target problem [46-48]. Although action masking and semantic rule – based inference have demonstrated effectiveness in other sequential decision-making tasks, their integration into microgrid optimization remains limited. Existing DRL-based energy management studies typically rely on numerical states alone and lack mechanisms for embedding semantic rules or feasibility constraints.
1.3 Research Objectives
This study will establish a real-time load demand dataset for a virtual building cluster, primarily based on campus building energy consumption data and combined with EV charging load data and data from other types of buildings. Optimize the operation of energy management systems within power supply environments incorporating photovoltaics, energy storage, and the grid. The research content of this study is as follows.
(1) Building a framework for generating charging pile load datasets: This study will utilize historical electricity consumption data from multi-site charging regions. Based on the data’s distribution characteristics and time series features, it will select appropriate statistical modeling methods. By combining scenario settings and individual variations, a framework will be established to generate real-time charging region load datasets.
(2) Building a Semantic mask DRL architecture with integrated environmental perception: By precisely sensing key environmental information (e.g., real-time electricity prices) and encoding semantic rules, the system proactively trims ineffective action spaces and avoids physically infeasible decisions. This enhances the rationality of the DRL model’s decisionmaking and the stability of the training process. Ultimately achieve an energy management strategy that balances economic efficiency and stability while meeting operational constraints.
(3) A multidimensional analysis and evaluation process: To comprehensively and accurately assess optimization strategy overall performance, this study will quantify their economic and environmental benefits under dynamic electricity pricing via core metrics (total system operating costs, total grid electricity purchases). It will evaluate training stability and decision reliability by counting invalid actions and analyzing reward trends, and finally assess shortterm power outage response capacity based on real-time available residual power.
This study will be mainly divided into six parts. The second part will focus on data analysis, the charging pile data generation process, and environment construction. The third part will cover the description of microgrid operation optimization strategies and experimental design. The fourth part is the analysis of the generation and optimization results. The fifth and sixth parts will be the discussion and conclusion respectively.
2. Data Analysis and Modeling Process
2.1 Energy Consumption Data Sources and Analysis for Building Cluster Microgrids
Due to restrictions on the confidentiality of operational data, it is difficult to obtain power consumption data for different types of buildings and charging regions within the same timeframe and geographical area. To this end, this study will construct a virtual building cluster and conduct research on the operation optimization of community microgrids, with real-time data as the main source and public datasets as supplementary sources. Most building energy consumption data comes from campus buildings. Campus buildings, characterized by complex functionality, frequent fluctuations in energy demand, and high real-time consumption requirements, have become a key focus in current microgrid optimization research [49, 50].

Based on the location of charging scenarios, charging stations can be categorized into home charging stations, workplace charging stations, and public charging stations [52]. The real-time electricity consumption data collected from charging regions in this study primarily originates from workplaces and public areas across multiple cities in China. However, due to location differences, there are significant variations in the usage frequency and real-time electricity consumption of individual charging piles [53]. As shown in the Fig.3, only a few areas exhibit higher average energy consumption for charging piles, which indirectly reflects that charging piles in these areas are used more frequently. Subsequently, a real-time electricity consumption model for charging stations will be constructed using actual data and deployed within a virtual building cluster. The entire community and microgrid will be set in the city with the largest building type in terms of electricity consumption (Liaoning Province, China). Environmental parameters such as temperature and solar radiation will utilize real-time data from the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF).
2.2 Real-Time Data Generation Process for Charging Piles
Based on real operational data from charging piles, this study aims to develop an energy consumption data generation framework for charging piles that not only captures the collective energy consumption patterns of regional charging piles but also accommodates scenariospecific settings and individual heterogeneities among charging piles. The charging pile dataset collected in this study spans a 30-day period. Since the charging piles corresponding to this dataset are distributed across multiple cities in China, the data exhibits significant geographical heterogeneity, making direct fitting unable to characterize the typical charging behavior features of a single charging pile. Moreover, the data volume varies across different charging piles. Therefore, this study needs to categorize the data along the temporal dimension and calculate the mean values to construct a baseline energy consumption dataset for individual charging piles, which serves as the foundation for subsequent model fitting and data generation.
It is assumed in this study that all charging piles within the virtual building cluster exhibit consistency in their hourly energy consumption trends, which can approximately characterize the typical charging behavior features across different time periods. The variation in energy consumption among charging piles primarily stems from two factors: geographical location (charging region) differences and random individual variations at the level of individual charging piles. Based on this assumption, this study adopts two fitting paradigms for feature fitting on the standardized dataset. The first paradigm is hourly probability distribution fitting (one model per hour), which includes three methods, the Normal distribution, the Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) and Kernel Density Estimation (KDE). The second paradigm is temporal trend fitting, which employs the Seasonal Autoregressive Integrated Moving Average (SARIMA) model.
Simulated power sequences matching the duration of the original data are generated based on each fitted model, and the method with the optimal fitting performance for the characteristic features of the original data is selected as the core method by calculating the Root Mean Square Error (RMSE). A global power adjustment coefficient and a scenario adjustment coefficient are assigned to each charging pile, and a systematic difference coefficient at the regional level is additionally introduced. Meanwhile, scenario no-charging probabilities differentiated by weekdays and weekends are synthesized based on the noisy-OR rule, which serves to determine whether a charging pile is in the charging state. The specific process is illustrated in the Fig.4, and the implementation logic of the four fitting methods and the configuration process of the scenario-based rules will be elaborated on in detail in the following sections. This study deploys 50 charging piles in a virtual urban area, which are evenly distributed across 10 charging regions.

2.3 Modeling of PV Energy Storage Microgrids
Based on relevant literature, this study models PV and energy storage systems and determines their associated parameters [13, 64-66]. Distributed PV systems represent a vital clean energy technology for converting solar energy into electricity. They are widely adopted due to their economic benefits and environmental friendliness.
Lithium batteries, as high-energy electrochemical energy storage devices, can store highquality electrical energy and are effectively applied in distributed power grids. The energy storage system capacity configured in this study can meet at least two hours of average operational demand [65]. Meanwhile, the supply and demand of the power system will achieve balance at different times. The operational rule for PV power generation prioritizes supply to the user side, with surplus power fed into the energy storage system. However, PV output is far lower than the user-side energy demand, meaning PV power is exclusively used to supply the user side in practical operation. For details on the relevant modeling process, please refer to Appendix A. This study will primarily discuss the operational costs that can be reduced through optimization in microgrid systems. The total cost primarily includes electricity procurement costs, battery equivalent degradation costs, and fixed operation and maintenance costs for photovoltaic systems and energy storage systems.
Actual electricity consumption is continuous, but in this study, it is recorded hourly. Therefore, the electricity rate used is based on the rate within the preceding hour. If two different rates apply within that hour, the most recent rate is used for calculation. The electricity price ratio is 1.5:1:0.5, with the flat-rate electricity price set at $0.1/kWh in this study. The equivalent degradation cost per unit energy of the battery will be determined based on relevant literature [67]. The service life of photovoltaic systems and energy storage systems shall be set according to the referenced literature [66]. The relevant cost calculation process is detailed in Appendix B.

3.2 Environmental Perception and Semantic Masking DQN
(1) Deep Q-networks
DQN represent an approach that combines reinforcement learning with artificial neural networks, primarily by extrapolating past experiences to new situations through interaction with the environment [68]. DQN use state and action spaces to determine optimal actions that maximize cumulative reward. Due to its simplicity and applicability, DQN has been refined and applied in numerous studies [69, 70]. For the detailed calculation process related to DQN, please refer to Appendix C.
(2) Environmental perception and semantic masking
